    Part D · Backend services

    Realtime

    Row changes and broadcasts to clients: the edge's realtime hub, its protocol, persisted topics, and the session-mode connection it listens on.

    Checked against bec3e57 · 2026-10-29
    The code has moved: 29 commits since
    • docs/decisions.md
    • internal/edge/edge.go
    • internal/edge/realtime.go
    • internal/edge/rtbroadcast.go
    • internal/edge/rthub.go
    • internal/edgeapi/edgeapi.go
    • internal/services/schema.go
    • internal/store/queries/services.sql
    • test/integration/realtime_test.go

    Realtime is the part of backend services that pushes to clients over a WebSocket: row changes from chosen tables, broadcasts between clients, and presence (V4 §6). There is no realtime package. xenibase-edge serves it from four files in internal/edge: the connection and its channels (realtime.go), the per-project hub and change feed (rthub.go), the wire format and filters (rtproto.go), and broadcast, presence and history (rtbroadcast.go). xenibase-server keeps the limits and clears what the edge leaves behind (internal/services/realtime.go). Everything realtime stores lives in the project's own database, in the xb_realtime schema. Delivery is at most once: a client that was away refetches.

    Which tables send changes#

    A table sends changes once its owner or the dashboard turns realtime on for it. xb_realtime.enable(regclass), created by schema version 5 in schema.go, refuses anything that is not a table, tables in xb_*, pg_*, information_schema and xenibase, a caller who does not own the table, and a table without a primary key. It then installs one AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE … FOR EACH ROW trigger, xb_realtime_capture, with the primary key columns as its arguments, and records the table and its key in xb_realtime.tables. disable drops both. The dashboard calls them as the platform through SetRealtimeTable (PUT …/realtime/tables/{schema}/{table}, action project.realtime_manage, developer and above).

    There is no publication, no replication slot and no logical decoding. The trigger writes to an outbox in the changing transaction, so a rolled-back change never appears:

    • What is stored. record is the whole new row. old_record holds only the primary key columns, so an update never carries the previous values out. xid defaults to pg_current_xact_id(), and at to now(), the transaction's start, which clients receive as commit_timestamp.
    • Who may write it. capture is SECURITY DEFINER, and only the edge login has SELECT on xb_realtime.outbox. No request role can read it or insert into it, so a client cannot forge a change.
    • The wake-up. Each captured row also runs pg_notify('xb_realtime', ''). Postgres folds identical notifications in one transaction into one, so a bulk insert wakes the edge once.
    • Clean-up. sweepRealtime deletes outbox rows older than 5 minutes, relayed messages older than 2 minutes and history older than 7 days, as the platform, on the 5-minute storage sweep, for every active project with schema version 5.

    How the edge learns what is on: the edge feed (feed.go) carries the project, its keys, its exposed schemas and the realtime limits, but not the list of tables. The hub reads xb_realtime.tables itself (tableKeys) and caches it for 3 seconds. A join for a table not in the cached list reads it again at once, so a table just turned on can be subscribed to without waiting.

    The hub and the listening connection#

    Each edge process has one rtHub per project, made on first use and kept for the life of the process. It holds the project's open connections, their joined channels (by topic) and the channels' subscriptions (by schema.table), the connection count and message counter for metering, the outbox cursor, and the broadcast and presence state. The first channel to join on a project starts listen, whatever the channel is for. It runs until the hub has had no channels for 30 seconds (rtLinger), so a reconnecting client finds it still there, or until the project leaves the feed (stop, below). A listener started after a stopped one waits for it to finish, since the cursor is the listener's own.

    listen opens a session-mode connection (sessionConn) as the project's edge login, through the region's session pooler on :5432, whose address the feed carries (or SessionAddr overrides). A transaction-mode pooler cannot hold LISTEN. In session mode PgBouncer gives that client a server connection of its own for as long as it stays, so each project with realtime clients costs one backend connection per edge process, on the project's session pool. Without a session pooler in the feed the hub polls the outbox every second through the ordinary transaction-mode pool instead.

    serve runs LISTEN xb_realtime; LISTEN xb_realtime_bc, sets the cursor, then loops: wait up to a second for a notification, read the outbox on a change notification or every second regardless, relay a broadcast notification from another edge process, and say hello to the others every 10 seconds.

    Reading the outbox in transaction order#

    The cursor is a low-water transaction id and a map of the transactions at or above it already read, with the last row of each (decision M34 #3). initCursor starts it at the current snapshot's xmin. Each drain takes a new snapshot and reads rows whose transaction is visible in it and not yet read:

    Everything below the new snapshot's xmin has finished, so the low-water mark moves up to it and older entries leave the map. A transaction still running at the snapshot is not visible yet and is read by a later drain. A long-running writer does not hold back later commits. The price is that delivery follows transaction ids, not strict commit order: two transactions that both commit between drains go out in the order they got their ids. When nobody on this edge subscribes to changes, drain just moves the mark to xmin and reads nothing.

    Each batch also drops the data API's cached reads of the tables it touched on this edge (dropCached, V4.1 §10), so every edge listening to a project invalidates its cache whatever wrote the rows.

    The WebSocket protocol#

    The wire format is the Phoenix channels protocol that Supabase's realtime clients speak, so they connect unchanged (decodeMsg, decision M34 #1). Version 1.0.0 sends each message as a JSON object and 2.0.0 (?vsn=2.0.0, or the first array a client sends) as [join_ref, ref, topic, event, payload]. A frame that is neither closes the connection.

    A client upgrades at /realtime/v1/websocket?apikey=…. The request goes through the gateway first, like any other (The data API): the hostname picks the project, the origin must be allowed, the key must be live, the per-IP and per-key rate limits apply, a suspended or paused project is refused, and so is a project whose organisation has used its month's API requests (planLimited) or that needs a second factor the token lacks. realtime then refuses the upgrade when the month's realtime messages are used up, when the organisation is at its spend cap, or past the connection limit. The connection's default identity is the key's role: service for the secret key, otherwise anon, or the user of a bearer token sent on the upgrade.

    EventWhat the edge does
    heartbeat on phoenixReplies ok. Any frame counts as a sign of life; after 2 minutes without one the connection is closed (idleLoop).
    phx_joinjoin: the topic must be realtime:<name>, at most 255 bytes. A join for a topic already joined replaces it. The payload is supabase-js's: config.broadcast.{self, ack}, config.presence.key (a random UUID if empty), config.private, config.postgres_changes, and an access_token.
    access_tokenChanges the channel's user (retoken), asking a private channel's policies again as the new user. An invalid token, or one whose user the policies refuse, closes the channel.
    broadcast, presenceAt most 600 a minute per connection together and 32 KB each, then a rate_limited or too_large error reply (below).
    phx_leaveLeaves the channel, replies ok, sends phx_close.

    A token in a join or access_token event is ignored on a secret-key connection, which stays service. Otherwise the publishable key itself (what supabase-js sends when signed out) keeps the connection's identity, and anything else must be a user's access token for this project: jwtes.Verify checks the signature against the project's keys, the audience (the ref) and expiry, the role must be user, and a project that requires a second factor refuses one below aal2. The channel remembers the token's exp, or, when it keeps the identity of a connection upgraded with a bearer token, that token's (setIdentity); such a connection cannot join a channel once its token has expired.

    Subscriptions and filters#

    Each postgres_changes entry becomes a subscription through bindChanges, at most 20 on a channel (rtMaxSubs) and 100 on a connection (rtMaxConnSubs), refused before any is checked. The event is *, INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE; the schema defaults to public; a table is required, since all tables at once is not supported. The table must have realtime on, be in an exposed schema, and be readable by the channel's role (has_table_privilege, checked as that role). Anon and users also need row-level security on it, or the table listed as public:

    A filter is column=op.value with eq, neq, lt, lte, gt, gte, or in.(a,b,…) up to 100 values (parseFilter), on a column the table has. It never reaches SQL: match compares it in Go against the row already read, numbers as numbers and anything else as text. There is no filter injection to have.

    A join that binds changes answers only once the hub's listener has its cursor (waitReady), so no change committed after "subscribed" is missed. The reply lists each subscription's id, which every postgres_changes message then names.

    Resolved

    Row-level security is checked on every batch, not only when a subscription is made. The table's RLS flag used to be read in bindChanges only, so after ALTER TABLE … DISABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY every existing anon or user subscription kept running its visibility query, which then returned every row, until it disconnected. visibleRows now applies the same rule for anon and users on a table not listed as public: it checks t.RLS from the catalogue it loads, then, since that is cached for up to 2 seconds, takes an ACCESS SHARE lock on the table and reads relrowsecurity itself, so the flag cannot change before the visibility query in the same transaction. When it is off, deliver drops that group's subscriptions (dropSubs) and sends each channel a system error naming the table; the channel stays joined for its broadcasts and presence, and the client subscribes again once security is back. TestRealtimeChangesStopWithoutRLS checks it against a project database.

    Authorising each change for each subscriber#

    deliver handles one batch from the outbox. It collects the subscriptions of each table touched and the primary keys of the inserted and updated rows. It groups the subscribers by fingerprint: the role, and for users every claim except exp, iat, nbf, jti and session_id, which is never wrong, only less shared than V4 §6.3's "claims that policies reference" (decision M34 #5). Each group runs one transaction as its own role's login with its claims (WithRequest, as the data API does), reading every changed row of that table at once:

    So yes, each row is checked as the subscriber's role, under the owner's policies and column grants, once per group per batch. What a subscriber receives as record is that query's row, the row as it is now, not the outbox copy. An insert followed quickly by a delete reaches nobody. An update that moves a row out of a subscriber's sight reaches them as nothing. columns carries the table's column types for the clients' conversions. Then, per change and per subscription: the event must match, the filter must pass on the visible row, and one message goes to each channel with the ids of its matching subscriptions.

    Deletes cannot be checked: the row is gone. Each subscription keeps a set of the primary keys it was sent, up to 10,000, and a connection's subscriptions up to 20,000 between them, oldest out first (pkSet; a set that adds past the connection's bound lets its own oldest go), and a delete goes, as the primary key only, to subscriptions whose set holds the key (decision M34 #6). A subscriber who joined after the row was last sent never hears of its delete; TestRealtime checks that with a later subscriber.

    Changes from another project cannot arrive: a hub reads only its own project's database, through that project's logins, and the token's audience must be the project's ref.

    Limits keep the checks affordable. Past 100 groups on a table (MaxGroups; the groups are sorted by fingerprint, so always the same ones), and when a group's query fails or times out, those subscribers get a system message resync instead. Past 200 changes a second per project on this edge (allow), the rest of that second's batches are not delivered and each affected subscription is told to resync once. The groups' queries run one after another in the listener goroutine, so a slow policy delays every subscriber of the project on that edge, and the relay of broadcasts from other edges with them.

    A user's token is checked for expiry in deliver, fanOut and presenceDiff before anything is sent, on every broadcast or presence update the channel sends, and every 10 seconds by the connection's own timer (recheck): a channel whose token has expired gets an error and is closed (expire). A client keeps a channel by sending access_token with a fresh token before then.

    Broadcasts, private channels and presence#

    A broadcast from a client (broadcastFrom) needs an event. It is sent at once to this edge's channels on the same topic with the same privacy (self decides whether the sender hears its own), acknowledged when the channel asked for ack, relayed to the project's other edge processes, and kept as history if its topic is persisted. First it must fit the project's budget on this process (budget): at most 32 KB (rtMaxMessage), at most 1 MB a second of broadcasts and presence from all the project's clients (rtBytesPerSecond), and on a persisted topic at most 256 KB of history a minute (rtHistoryBytesPerMinute); otherwise the sender gets a too_large or rate_limited error reply and nobody gets the message. Servers broadcast over HTTP with the secret key: POST /realtime/v1/api/broadcast, 1 to 100 messages of at most 32 KB each, a body of at most 256 KB, under the same budget (429 with how many were sent).

    A public channel is open to anyone with the publishable key, for reading and writing. A private channel (config.private) is decided by the owner's policies on xb_realtime.channel_access, a table the owner owns with row-level security on. channelAccess probes them as the channel's role in a transaction it rolls back, once for broadcast and once for presence: xb_realtime.probe (security definer) inserts a row for the topic, a SELECT as the caller decides whether they see it (may receive), and an INSERT as the caller decides whether their policies let them add one (may send). A user who may receive neither is refused the join. The secret key passes. The policies are asked again when the channel's token changes and, by recheck, every minute (rtRecheck): a user they now refuse is closed out, what they allow replaces the channel's flags (a user no longer allowed to track presence loses theirs), and while the database cannot be reached the flags stay as they were. A private and a public channel of the same name never hear each other: broadcasts and presence are keyed by topic and privacy (topicKey).

    Presence (presenceFrom) keeps one entry per channel: track replaces the channel's earlier entry with the client's payload plus a new phx_ref, and untrack or leaving removes it. Every joiner gets presence_state, and the topic's channels get presence_diff for each change. The presence key is whatever the client says; on a public channel nothing stops two clients choosing the same one.

    Resolved

    Authorisation is no longer decided only at join, and token expiry holds for broadcast and presence too. channelAccess ran in join only, so a member removed from a room kept receiving its private broadcasts and presence until they left, and access_token swapped the identity without asking the policies; expiry was checked only in deliver, and a channel on a connection upgraded with a bearer token never expired at all, since setToken took exp only from a token it parsed. Now the expiry comes from the upgrade's claims too; fanOut and presenceDiff skip and close a channel whose token has expired, as does a broadcast or presence update it sends, and the connection's 10-second timer closes the rest; access_token asks a private channel's policies as the new user before switching to it; and every minute each private channel's policies are asked again. The flags are kept under the channel's lock with the identity they were asked for. TestRealtimeTokenExpiry and, against a project database, TestRealtimePrivateChannelsRechecked check it. Between checks a removed member still hears the room for up to a minute.

    Persisted topics#

    The owner lists topics whose broadcasts are kept for 7 days in xb_realtime.persisted_topics, directly or through SetPersistedTopics (at most 100 topics). The edge caches the list for 10 seconds (persisted), and persist inserts each broadcast on a listed topic into broadcast_history as the edge login, with the sender's user id and whether it was sent on the private channel (private, schema version 9). Clients read it back with GET /realtime/v1/history/<topic>?after=&limit=, the public channel's, or with private=true the private channel's:

    Resolved

    A private topic's history is no longer readable with the publishable key. persist kept private and public broadcasts alike under the bare topic name, and history checked channel_access only when the query said private=true, then filtered by topic alone, so GET /realtime/v1/history/vip with just the publishable key returned every message members had sent on the private vip channel for 7 days, sender ids included. Schema version 9 adds private to broadcast_history; persist writes the sending channel's privacy, and the history query always filters by it, so the plain request reads only the public channel's history and private=true reads the private one's after the read policy (the secret key passes, which it did not before: channelAccess returned early for it without setting the flags, so the secret key's private history answered 403). Rows from before version 9, which do not say, became private, the column's default: their public broadcasts are readable only through the topic's read policy or the secret key until they expire. TestRealtimeHistoryKeepsPrivateApart checks each case against a project database. Anon may still read a public channel's history on any persisted topic.

    Several edge processes, reconnects and missed messages#

    Every edge process listening to a project reads the whole outbox itself and delivers to its own clients, so row changes need no coordination between processes. Broadcasts and presence do, and go through the project's own database (decision M34 #8). relayOut sends pg_notify('xb_realtime_bc', …) through the transaction pool, but only while this process has a listening connection and has heard another process say hello in the last 35 seconds. A message over 7,800 bytes, which one NOTIFY cannot carry, is split into parts that each fit (splitRelay, base64 with the message's id and each part's number) and sent as the notifications of one statement, so nothing is written to a table or the WAL; relayIn holds parts for up to 10 seconds and 16 MB until the message is whole (joinPart). Only a message over 1,000 parts, about 5 MB (a large topic's presence state, which sendState now sends a topic at a time), is still written to xb_realtime.relay with only its id sent:

    relayIn ignores its own messages, fans out broadcasts, applies presence diffs, answers a newcomer's hello with its own hello and full presence state (pst), and drops a process that says goodbye. A process not heard for 35 seconds is dropped with its clients' presence (expirePeers), which is how a crashed process's users leave. TestRealtimeNodeLoss kills one of two processes with SIGKILL and checks just that. Without a session pooler there is no listening connection, and broadcasts and presence stay within each process.

    There is no replay. A client that disconnects misses what happened meanwhile and refetches when it rejoins; Xenibase's SDKs do this for live queries. When the hub's own listening connection drops, listen reconnects with a backoff from 1 to 30 seconds, sends every change subscriber resync (resyncAll) and starts a new cursor, so the changes in between are skipped rather than delivered late.

    Resolved

    The publishable key can no longer make the edge write large broadcasts into the project's database. A public channel needs no authorisation to send, a frame could be 256 KB and a connection could send 600 broadcasts a minute; once a second edge process listened to the project, every broadcast over 7,800 bytes became an xb_realtime.relay row, about 150 MB a minute per connection through the shared cluster's WAL, and on a persisted public topic a broadcast_history row for 7 days. Now a broadcast or presence message is at most 32 KB, the project's clients may send at most 1 MB a second of them through each edge process, and a persisted topic keeps at most 256 KB a minute per process; past these the sender gets an error reply and the message goes nowhere. A large message reaches the other processes as NOTIFY parts, which are not WAL-logged, so relay rows are left for messages over about 5 MB, which only a large presence state can reach. TestRealtimeBroadcastLimits and TestRealtimeRelayParts check the limits and the parts, and TestRealtimeBroadcastsSpareTheDatabase checks against a project database that no relay row is written and how much history is kept.

    Metering: every 10 seconds meterRealtime adds each hub's open connections times the seconds elapsed, and the messages counted since, to the edge's hourly usage report. xenibase-server records them as realtime_connection_minutes and realtime_messages, which billing rates past the plan's allowance (Billing, Free tier and capacity) and the realtime sweep compares with the monthly limit. A message is a broadcast or presence update a client sends (handle), each broadcast, presence update or change queued to a client (send), and each HTTP broadcast; the protocol around them is not counted (below).

    Resolved

    Heartbeats are no longer billed as messages. run counted every frame read and send every message queued, heartbeats and their phx_reply among them, so a connection that did nothing cost about 207,000 messages a month: five idle browser tabs used up a Personal organisation's 1,000,000. Both now count only what billable accepts: broadcasts, presence updates, presence_state, presence_diff and postgres_changes, on any topic but phoenix. Heartbeats, joins, leaves, access_token, replies (acks included), phx_close and system messages are free. TestRealtimeCountsOnlyMessages checks it.

    Resolved

    The Personal plan's monthly message limit now stops connections already open. MessagesBlocked was read once, in realtime, before the upgrade, though the edgeapi field said it also stopped delivery, and the same held for an organisation that had used its month's API requests: a free project's clients that stayed connected kept sending and receiving for the rest of the month, metered on a plan with no overage to bill. Both flags are now part of refusal, so when the sweep sets one and the feed brings it, feedChanged closes the project's connections with the reason (and each connection's 10-second check would within that time); their reconnects are refused at the gateway. The HTTP broadcast is refused with 429 realtime_quota_exceeded too. The flag itself is still set by the 5-minute realtime sweep from the usage the edges report, so a project can pass the limit by a few minutes of use first. TestRealtimeMonthlyLimitsCloseConnections checks it, and that a spend cap leaves connections open.

    Resolved

    Memory per connection is bounded. A join could bind any number of postgres_changes entries and a connection hold 100 channels, each subscription's seen set growing to 10,000 keys (about 600 KB), so anyone with the publishable key on a table anon may read and insert into could make the edge hold gigabytes for one client; the send queue added up to 256 messages of up to 256 KB, and presence a 256 KB payload per channel on every process. Now a channel binds at most 20 subscriptions and a connection 100 (V4 §6.3's "subscribers per channel"), a connection's subscriptions remember at most 20,000 keys between them (about 1.2 MB), a frame is at most 64 KB and a broadcast or presence message 32 KB, and the send queue is bounded at 4 MB as well as 256 messages (a single larger change still goes when nothing else is waiting). TestRealtimeSubscriptionCaps, TestRealtimeSeenKeysBounded, TestRealtimeFrameLimit and TestRealtimeSendQueueBytes check each. The set also no longer lets a key go early when it was removed by a delete and sent again.

    Spec and code differ

    V4 §10.1 gives a plan's connections per project. The code enforces them per edge process (decision M34 #11), so a project gets the limit times the number of edge processes in its region. V4 §6.3 lists "subscribers per channel" and "groups checked per change (plan limit)" as limits; the code limits a channel's subscriptions (and a connection's), and the group limit is 100 on every plan.

    When the project or its key changes#

    The gateway's checks run at the upgrade, and the connection remembers the key it was opened with. Whenever the feed brings a project's entry (a change, or the full resync every minute), apply hands its ref to feedChanged, which closes each open connection that refusal no longer allows: the project has left the feed (services off, deleted or moved), it is not active (its organisation suspended, or paused), its organisation has used the month's realtime messages (MessagesBlocked) or API requests (RequestsBlocked), or the connection's key is no longer one of the project's. Each channel gets a system error and the socket closes with 1008 and the reason; the client's reconnect then meets the gateway. When the project has left the feed the hub also closes its channels and stops the listener at once (stop), closing its session-pooler connection. Each connection's 10-second timer (recheck) applies the same refusal, as a backstop. A spend cap still leaves open connections alone (V4 §12).

    Resolved

    Open WebSockets no longer outlive a revoked key, a suspended organisation or services turned off. Nothing in the hub read the feed after the upgrade: a connection opened with a since-revoked secret key kept its service identity, every subscription and the right to join private channels for as long as it sent heartbeats; a suspended organisation's connections carried on; and when services were turned off, broadcasts and the session-pooler connection stayed until that connection happened to fail. Now apply tells the hub of every feed entry it takes, feedChanged closes the connections refusal no longer allows, and a project that has left the feed has its listener stopped at once; every connection also checks itself every 10 seconds. A failed serve no longer retries at once in a loop either: it waits a second (the poll without a session pooler failed fast against an unreachable database). TestRealtimeConnectionsFollowTheFeed checks the closes over real WebSockets, and TestRealtimeListenerStopsWithTheProject, against a project database, that the listener and its connection go and a listener starts again when the project returns.

    Failure handling#

    What failsWhat happens
    The listening connection dropslisten reconnects after a second, backing off from 1 to 30 seconds while it cannot connect, then sends every change subscriber resync and starts a new cursor. Broadcasts from other processes are missed meanwhile.
    No session pooler in the feedThe outbox is polled every second through the transaction pool. Broadcasts and presence stay within each edge process.
    The database is unreachable when a client joins with changesThe join waits up to 15 seconds for the listener, then answers ok anyway. Changes committed before the listener's first cursor are missed without a resync, since the first connection does not send one.
    A read of the outbox failsWith a listening connection that has closed, as a lost connection. Otherwise logged; the cursor has not moved, so the next drain reads the same rows.
    The edge cannot read the outbox for over 5 minutesThe sweep deletes the rows unread. Subscribers got resync on the reconnect.
    A group's visibility query fails or times out (10 seconds, or the statement timeout)That group's subscribers get resync for the batch.
    More than 100 groups, or more than 200 changes a secondThe groups past the hundredth, or the second's remaining batches, get resync; their changes are not delivered.
    A table subscribed to by anon or users loses row-level securityAt its next change, those subscriptions are dropped with a system error; their changes are not delivered.
    A user's token expiresAn error and the channel closed: at the next change, broadcast or presence update due to it or sent by it, or within 10 seconds.
    A private channel's policies cannot be asked againLogged; the channel keeps what they allowed and is asked again at the next tick.
    A client reads too slowlyAfter 256 queued messages or 4 MB, or a write taking 10 seconds, the connection is closed; the client reconnects and refetches.
    A client stops sendingClosed after 2 minutes without a frame; its presence leaves.
    An edge process diesIts clients reconnect to another. Their presence leaves the others within 35 seconds. Usage it had not yet reported is lost.
    A relayed message's parts don't all arrive within 10 seconds, or its row is gone (over 2 minutes), or the notify or relay insert failsThe message is dropped for the other processes; local clients already had it.
    A history insert failsLogged; the broadcast was already delivered.
    The project leaves the feed, its organisation is suspended, or a connection's key is revokedThe connections it no longer allows are closed with 1008 when the feed brings the change, or within 10 seconds; leaving the feed also stops the listener.

    The tests: TestRealtime (two users each seeing only their rows, a rolled-back insert, updates, deletes to earlier subscribers only, filters, refused subscriptions), TestRealtimeBroadcast (broadcast and presence across two processes, private channels, history, the HTTP broadcast, the rate cap, the connection limit, metering), TestRealtimeNodeLoss, and TestRealtimeLoad, 10,000 connections on one edge.

    Spec and code differ

    Smaller differences, most recorded under V4-M34 in docs/decisions.md. V4 §6.5 relays between edge processes over LISTEN/NOTIFY on the metadata database; the code uses the project's own database. §6.2 and §6.4 read and deliver "in commit order"; the code reads in transaction-id order. §6.3 step 2 runs SELECT 1 and delivers the change; the code delivers the row as the subscriber reads it at delivery time. §6.1 offers eq and in filters; the code also has neq, lt, lte, gt and gte. §11.2 grants request roles SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on channel_access; they get SELECT and INSERT.

    A webhook POSTs the row changes of chosen tables to a URL; a scheduled job runs SQL or calls a URL on a cron schedule. Both are a tenant's way of making Xenibase send traffic, so both go through one hardened outbound client, and both pause while a project is not itself able to serve. The configuration and logs live in the metadata database; the webhook queue lives in the project's own database as a transactional outbox. Only xenibase-server delivers, under a fleet-wide lock, so plaintext secrets and tenant rows never leave the server that holds them.

    The outbox in the project's database#

    Saving the first webhook installs a xenibase schema in the project's database: the webhook_outbox table and a trigger function, both owned by the superuser (outboxDDL). Each watched table gets a row trigger that writes every change to the outbox in the same transaction as the change, so a rolled-back change never produces an event and a committed one always does (V2 §9.1). An outbox row holds the webhook id, the qualified table name, the operation, and old_row and new_row as jsonb, plus the attempt count, next-attempt time and last error.

    The schema belongs to Xenibase, not the tenant. REVOKE ALL takes the schema, the table and the function away from PUBLIC, so the project role cannot read the outbox, insert into it, or call the function. The function is SECURITY DEFINER with its search_path pinned to pg_catalog, pg_temp, and the triggers are created by the superuser, so the project role cannot attach the function to its own tables with a forged webhook id. The schema name is reserved: outboxDDL first drops any xenibase schema (or object in it) owned by anyone but the superuser, so a tenant's squat, or a copy a restore brought back as the project role, can never stand in for Xenibase's own (V2 §9.1, decision M15 #1).

    Why the outbox is not a tamper vector

    The delivery worker reads table_name and the row JSON straight from the outbox, but a tenant cannot write a row there, so it cannot make Xenibase send to an arbitrary address or carry another table's data: the destination is the webhook's stored URL (re-checked at delivery), and the only way into the outbox is the superuser-owned trigger on a table the tenant owns. The function builds the payload with to_jsonb(OLD/NEW); because to_jsonb on a composite recurses to built-in scalar types and ignores tenant-defined casts on composite or domain types (a base type's I/O needs the superuser), a column of a tenant type cannot smuggle a function that would run with the definer's rights.

    Draining the outbox#

    Run takes one fleet-wide advisory lock (pg_try_advisory_lock), so exactly one xenibase-server is the deliverer; the others retry the lock every ten seconds. The holder runs one loop per project with webhooks (supervise), each on its own connection with LISTEN xenibase_webhooks to wake on commit, plus a five-second poll. A pass reads each webhook's head events in id order, LIMIT 100, and sends them one at a time; a head event that is waiting for its retry, or that fails, holds back the rest of that webhook's queue but not other webhooks. A delivered or dead-lettered row is deleted from the outbox and recorded in webhook_deliveries; a failed row keeps its place with a new next_attempt_at. Delivery is at-least-once (the send, the log row and the outbox delete are separate statements), so receivers de-duplicate on the stable Xenibase-Event-Id.

    The event id is evt_<webhook>_<outbox id>, stable across retries and kept by a replay. committed_at is the change's transaction time. When old_row and new_row together exceed 256 KB the body carries no rows, only the primary key and "truncated": true (body).

    Spec and code differ

    V2 §9.1 step 6 says the worker reads outbox rows "with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED". The code does not: head reads with a plain ORDER BY id LIMIT, and concurrency is prevented instead by the single fleet-wide delivery lock plus one loop per project. The effect the spec wants (no two workers sending the same event) holds; the mechanism is different, and the outbox connection is Xenibase's own, not the tenant's.

    The outbound client: no SSRF, no rebinding#

    Every webhook delivery and HTTP job goes through internal/outbound, the only path by which a tenant makes Xenibase send a request. Check parses the URL (no userinfo, https:// only unless the host is allow-listed), resolves it once, and requires every resolved address to be public, so a name cannot mix a public address with an internal one.

    Link-local and cloud-metadata ranges (169.254.0.0/16, fe80::/10, fd00:ec2::254) are refused even for an allow-listed host, and canon maps IPv4-mapped, NAT64 and 6to4 addresses to the IPv4 they embed so 64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe is still caught as 169.254.169.254. The checked address is pinned: transport dials only that netip.AddrPort, with no proxy, so a second DNS lookup cannot rebind the name between the check and the connection. Send does not follow redirects (http.ErrUseLastResponse), bounds the call by a 10-second timeout, and keeps only the first 4 KB of the response as a snippet. A webhook batch is checked once by Prepare (gate, allow-list, DNS) and every event in the batch goes to that one checked address.

    The allow-list is per organisation and set by the platform admin only. Each request is counted per organisation and destination host, host and counts only, written about once a second and swept after 30 days (SweepOutboundCounters). An organisation that is suspended or has outbound traffic turned off is refused by Gate; its deliveries then queue in the outbox.

    Signatures, secrets and rotation#

    A webhook's signing secret (whsec_…) and any static headers are sealed with the master key (secretAAD, headersAAD) and shown once. Each request carries Xenibase-Signature: t=<unix>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of "t.body"> (signature.mac); the timestamp is the wall clock at send, and the receiver checks it against a tolerance to refuse replays. The signing package has no dependencies, so xenibase-status can verify the same scheme. Nothing in the delivery log keeps the secret: it records the URL, status, latency and the receiver's own response snippet.

    RotateSecret replaces the secret and, with an overlap of up to 24 hours, keeps the previous one signing alongside the new one (two v1 values) until it expires, so a receiver can switch without failing events in flight. PreviousSecret drops the old secret the moment the overlap ends.

    Retries, dead letters and failure emails#

    The outcome decides the row's fate. A 2xx succeeds. A 429, a 5xx or a network error retries; any other 4xx, a 3xx (redirects are not followed), and a destination refused at send time (its DNS changed to an internal address) dead-letter at once.

    backoff doubles from 10 seconds to at most 2 hours with ±20% jitter, about 20 attempts over 24 hours; once a retry would land past 24 hours from the change the event is dead-lettered instead. A dead letter keeps its payload and is visible in the UI, replayable singly or in bulk by Replay, which re-queues it after the waiting events, keeping the original event id. Fifty consecutive failed deliveries pause the webhook, disable its triggers and email the project's admins and the organisation's owners (recordHealth). A minute's health check also marks a webhook broken if the tenant dropped or disabled its triggers (checkTriggers), rather than re-creating them silently.

    The delivery log is swept after 7 days, dead letters not replayed after 30 (SweepDeliveries). The outbox lives in the project's own database and so counts against its storage quota; if it passes 100,000 rows the admins are emailed once (health). Because a paused webhook stops enqueuing, and because events older than 24 hours dead-letter fast and quickly trip the 50-failure pause, a down receiver bloats the outbox for at most about a day before the webhook auto-pauses.

    Restore, branch, move and delete#

    Webhooks are configuration in the metadata database; the outbox is data in the project's database. What happens to the outbox on a lifecycle event is Reinstall and Strip, wired through provision.ResetWebhooks.

    EventWhat happens to the outbox and triggers
    Restore in place, branch resetThe xenibase schema that came with the data is dropped and rebuilt from Xenibase's configuration with an empty outbox, so events from the restored past are not replayed (V2 §9.3).
    New branch, restore into a new project, import, point-in-time recoveryThe schema is stripped; the new project keeps no webhooks (copies do not carry them, V2 §8.1). A project that has its own webhooks gets them rebuilt empty.
    Move, promotion, demotionThe outbox and triggers move with the data (the xenibase schema is copied as the superuser, copyKeepingOwners); delivery pauses while the project is not active and resumes after, so no event is lost (docs/moves.md).
    DeleteDropAutomation deletes the project's webhooks and jobs from the metadata database; the project's database is torn down with the outbox in it.

    Delivery only runs for live, active projects (WebhookProjects): a suspended organisation, an inactive-tier (paused) project, or an organisation at its spend cap all leave the events queued until they recover (V3 §3.10, §4.2).

    Scheduled jobs#

    internal/schedjobs runs a project's jobs on a 5-field cron schedule in an IANA time zone. Parse is Xenibase's own parser (ranges, lists, steps, day and month names, @daily and the other macros); it needs no dependency. Next walks forward in the schedule's location to the next matching minute, giving up after five years (so 30 February has no run). The plan's minimum interval is checked against MinGap, the shortest gap over the next 1,000 runs.

    A SQL job runs its script as the project owner, in one transaction, through the console login, which holds no privileges of its own, so the script cannot RESET ROLE its way to the superuser (console.RunJob). Unlike an admin connection, the job keeps the database's read-only default, so a soft storage lock applies to it.

    An HTTP job calls its URL through the same outbound client, signed with a per-job secret and a Xenibase-Job header (runHTTP). The schedule and request are validated at save time, and the request's headers may not set xenibase-*, host or content-length. Timeouts default to 5 minutes for SQL and 30 seconds for HTTP, capped at 1 hour.

    Run holds its own fleet-wide advisory lock, so one server schedules; Tick picks the due jobs every five seconds, sets each next run from now (a run missed during downtime is not caught up; at most one late run fires, then the schedule continues), and starts each in a goroutine. dispatch records a run and enforces the overlap policy: a job whose previous run is still going is skipped or queued for when it ends. The check and the insert run in one transaction holding the job's row (LockJob, FOR UPDATE), as does starting a queued run when the one before it ends, and partial unique indexes allow one running and one queued run per job.

    Runs that a stopped server left queued or running are failed on the next leader's start (FailInterruptedRuns). Three failures in a row email the admins. Run history is kept 30 days and at most 1,000 runs per job (SweepJobRuns).

    Resolved

    A daily job no longer runs twice, or never stops looking, at a DST change. Next stepped through wall-clock hours in the job's zone. When the clocks went back (America/New_York on 1 November 2026, when 01:00–02:00 occurs twice), a job at 30 1 * * * fired at 01:30 EDT and the next match was 01:30 EST an hour later, so it ran twice that day. When they went forward, a fixed time in the skipped hour was not merely missed: for 30 2 * * * in New York, time.Date normalised the missing 02:00 back to 01:00 EST, the walk went backwards, and Next looped for ever, hanging the scheduler's Tick and the save (whose MinGap looks a year ahead); in zones ahead of UTC the run was dropped for the day. Next now walks one zone period (from one offset change to the next, ZoneBounds) at a time, matching in plain UTC wall time inside it, where nothing repeats or is missing. A fixed-time schedule (minute and hour both given, not *) starts a period that follows a fall-back after the repeated stretch, so it fires at the first occurrence only; at a spring-forward it fires at the first minute after the gap if a time it matches fell in it (cronie's behaviour). Schedules with * in the minute or hour run by the clock through both. Every run is at least a minute after the one before. TestNextAcrossDST covers fixed-time, hourly and every-N-minute schedules across both 2026 changes in New York and London, and TestNextDSTYear a year of runs in five zones, including Lord Howe's half-hour shift and Santiago's at midnight.

    Resolved

    "Run now" no longer races the scheduler. dispatch used to read ActiveJobRuns and then insert a running row with nothing between the two, and RunJob calls RunNow on whichever API server serves the request, so a manual run that coincided with the scheduled one, or two manual runs on two servers, could both find no active run and both start: an overlap: skip job ran concurrently, and a queue job could start every request. A run queued just as the previous one finished could also be left waiting until the next leader failed it. The check and the insert now run in one transaction that first locks the job's row (LockJob), and the finishing run takes the same lock before it starts a queued one. Migration 00086 adds partial unique indexes on job_runs (job_id) for running and for queued rows, which both overlap policies allow at most one of, after failing any duplicates the race left. TestDispatchConcurrentSkip and TestDispatchConcurrentQueue dispatch each of many jobs from the scheduler and "Run now" at once and expect one run started (and, for queue, one queued) and the rest skipped; without the lock they start two or three.

    Limits, permissions and usage#

    Everything under webhooks and jobs is one authorization action, project.automation (developer and above, write token scope), reads included, because the reads show URLs and SQL; read-only members do not see them. Plan limits are per organisation (store limit keys), seeded in the quota plans:

    LimitPersonal (Free)ProTeamEnforced by
    Webhook deliveries per minute60120300A per-org token bucket; excess waits in the outbox (TakeFrom, seeded from the delivery log; returns errQueued).
    Scheduled jobs203050CountOrgJobs at create (409 quota_exceeded).
    Minimum interval (seconds)3006060MinGap at save, never below the 1-minute floor.
    HTTP job runs per hour120300600A count of the org's HTTP job runs in the last hour (CountOrgHTTPJobRuns, under a per-org advisory lock); excess runs are skipped and recorded.

    There is no cap on the number of webhooks (only on tables per webhook, 20); the Unlimited plan carries an empty limits map. The webhook token bucket lives in the delivering server's memory, which is consistent while one server holds the lock. A server that has no bucket for an organisation yet, such as a new leader after a failover or a restart, starts it with the attempts the delivery log already holds for the last minute spent (TakeFrom, CountOrgWebhookAttempts), so the handover does not hand out a fresh minute's allowance. The HTTP job limit used to be such a bucket too, in the memory of whichever server dispatched, so a new scheduler leader, and every API server serving "Run now", started with a full hour's allowance; it is now counted from job_runs in the dispatch transaction, so it holds across servers and failovers. Hourly usage is rolled up for billing: webhook_delivery_attempts, webhook_deliveries (successes), and SQL and HTTP job runs (HourlyWebhookDeliveries, HourlyJobRuns).

    Spec and code differ

    V2 §9.2 says a schedule's default time zone is "the creator's". validate defaults an empty time zone to UTC; the creator's zone is never read on the server. The UI can still send one.

    Failure handling#

    What failsWhat happens
    The receiver answers 429 or 5xx, times out, or the connection failsRetried with backoff (10s doubling to 2h, ±20% jitter) for up to 24 hours from the change, then dead-lettered.
    The receiver answers another 4xx, or a 3xx redirectDead-lettered at once (redirects are not followed).
    The URL's host now resolves to an internal addressRefused at delivery and dead-lettered; a create or save is refused up front (400).
    50 deliveries fail in a rowThe webhook is paused, its triggers disabled, and the admins and owners emailed. Queued events wait; new changes are not recorded until it is resumed.
    The tenant drops or disables a webhook's triggersThe minute's health check marks the webhook broken; saving it reinstalls them. Triggers are never re-created silently.
    The outbox passes 100,000 rowsThe admins are emailed once. Events are kept in the project's database until delivered, dead-lettered, or the webhook is deleted.
    The project is moving, restoring or resetting; the org is suspended or over its spend cap; outbound traffic is offDelivery and job runs wait (jobs record a skipped run with the reason); nothing is dropped.
    A SQL job exceeds its timeoutstatement_timeout cancels it; the run is timed_out with the error.
    An HTTP job's receiver answers non-2xxThe run is failed with the status code and response snippet.
    The previous run of a job is still goingskip records a skipped run; queue records a queued run that starts when the current one ends.
    The scheduler or delivery server stops mid-runA job run left running/queued is failed as interrupted on the next leader's start; webhook events stay in the outbox and are re-sent (at-least-once).
    A scheduled run is missed during downtimeNot caught up; the next time runs from now, and the history shows the gap. A fixed time the clocks skip at a spring-forward runs at the first minute after the gap; one in an hour that repeats runs once.
    A job's organisation reaches its spend capThe run is skipped with the reason; webhook deliveries queue.

    The broader plumbing these lean on is the The control plane queue and locks, Connections: poolers and the edge for the pooler the HTTP paths avoid, Project auth for the project.automation action, and Billing, Free tier and capacity for the spend cap and usage.
