    This page is about the people who use Xenibase itself: the platform admin, support staff, and the users who own and work in organisations. The users of an app built on Xenibase sign in through project auth, a different system in each project's own database (Project auth). The two share only internal/totp and internal/argonpw. Everything here lives in the metadata database and is served by xenibase-server's API, behind the guard described on The control plane.

    • auth2,288 linesImplements operator authentication (spec §7.2): argon2id passwords, TOTP second factor, server-side sessions, step-up re-authentication, and login rate limiting with lockout.
    • authz440 linesDecides who may do what (V2 §2.3–2.6).
    • orgs1,012 linesOrganisations, memberships, invitations, and project transfers (V2 §2–3).
    • tokens1,197 linesIssues and checks API tokens for the CLI, CI and scripts (V2 §7.2), and runs the device login that issues them to the CLI.
    • totp91 linesRFC 6238 one-time codes, shared by operator accounts and project users' second factors (V4 §4.1).
    • argonpw66 linesHashes passwords with argon2id in the PHC string format and verifies them in constant time.
    • mail818 linesSends Xenibase's email: account verification, password resets, invitations, and alerts (V2 §3.1).

    Who is who#

    A user has one login and may belong to many organisations. Each organisation owns its projects, tokens, storage targets, usage and audit log. A user's power comes from three layers, each stored in its own column:

    LayerRolesStored onGrants
    Platformplatform_admin, support, userusers.platform_rolePlatform routes; the support console. Nothing inside an organisation the user is not in.
    Organisationowner, admin, member, billingorg_members.roleOwners and admins are admin of every project. Members see only projects they were added to. Billing sees billing and no project.
    Projectadmin, developer, read_onlyproject_members.roleThe actions in projectMin.

    A request is made by one of three actors (authz.Actor): a browser session, an API token, or the system. A token is its user acting in one organisation, within its scopes and, optionally, only on some projects. The credentials a person can hold:

    CredentialFormStored asLifetime
    Password12 to 256 charactersargon2id, 64 MiB, 3 passes, 2 lanesUntil changed or reset
    TOTP secret160 bits, base32Sealed with the master key, bound to the user idUntil turned off or reset
    Recovery codes10 codes, xxxxx-xxxxxA sealed list of SHA-256 hashesSingle use each
    Session32 random bytes in a cookieSHA-256 in sessions12 hours idle, 7 days at most
    API tokenxb_ + 43 base62 charactersSHA-256 in api_tokens1 hour to 365 days, 90 by default
    Emailed link32 random bytesSHA-256 in email_tokens or invitationsVerification 48 hours, reset 1 hour, invitation 7 days

    Accounts and signup#

    The first account is made by the setup wizard. BeginSetup needs the setup code xenibase-server prints to its log, checks the password, and seals the email, hash and a fresh TOTP secret into a 15-minute challenge. Nothing exists until CompleteSetup gets a valid code: then, under an advisory lock, it creates the platform admin as verified and approved, their personal organisation, and their first session. Five wrong codes delete the challenge.

    After that, accounts come from signup or from invitations. The platform admin picks the signup mode (SetSignupPolicy, stored in settings under signup):

    ModePOST /auth/signupA new account
    invite_only (default)403 signup_closedOnly by accepting an invitation from the platform admin or from any organisation
    approvalAcceptedUnverified and unapproved; signs in once verified and approved by the platform admin (ApproveUser, which emails them)
    openAcceptedUnverified, approved at once

    Signup checks, in order: the mode; the address (parsable, at most 254 bytes); the domain allow-list, an exact match on the part after the last @; the anti-bot challenge and the per-IP cap (SignupGuard, in approval and open mode alike); the password; and the current terms version. Turnstile runs when its keys are set, and any failure, Cloudflare being unreachable included, refuses the signup (Turnstile.Verify). The cap is 3 accounts per signup_ip a day by default (XENIBASE_SIGNUPS_PER_IP).

    An address that already has an account gets an email saying so, and the request answers 202 as for a new one; the password is hashed first either way, so the two take as long. A new address gets a user row, a personal organisation (createPersonalOrg), a terms acceptance and a 48-hour verification link. emailToken retires earlier links of the same purpose, so only the newest works, and only once.

    A password is at least 12 runes and at most 256 bytes (CheckPasswordPolicy), with no complexity rule and no breached-password check. defaultArgon is argon2id at 64 MiB, 3 passes and 2 lanes (RFC 9106's second recommendation) in PHC form. argonpw.Verify reads the parameters from the hash, so project users' cheaper hashes verify with the same code.

    Signing in, TOTP and lockout#

    Sign-in is two calls. POST /auth/login runs Login. An unknown or disabled address verifies the password against a fixed dummy hash (dummyHash) and fails like a wrong password, counted and locked like one (addressFailure). Only the right password learns that the address is unverified or awaiting approval. A right password stores a 5-minute challenge, and then one of three things happens:

    • No second factor. An ordinary account without TOTP: the handler completes the challenge at once and the answer carries the session (loginResult).
    • TOTP. The answer carries a challenge id; POST /auth/totp sends it with a code to CompleteLogin.
    • Enrolment. Platform admins and support staff must have TOTP (totpRequired). Without one, the answer carries a new secret in a 15-minute enroll challenge, and the first valid code enrols it and returns the recovery codes.

    Ordinary accounts turn TOTP on under Account → Security with the password and a first code (EnableTOTP), and off with the password and a code (DisableTOTP, refused to platform staff). Both changes are emailed.

    Codes are RFC 6238 (HMAC-SHA1, 6 digits, 30 seconds, one step of drift; totp.Verify), and checkTOTP accepts only a step later than users.totp_last_step, so a code works once. Any 10-character input is taken as a recovery code, and useRecoveryCode removes it from the sealed list under a row lock. Regenerating the codes needs step-up.

    Two limits stand in the way of guessing:

    • Per address. auth.Limiter is a sliding window in memory, per process: 10 attempts per 5 minutes for sign-in, TOTP, step-up, signup, reset requests and password changes, and 60 per 5 minutes for requests that present an emailed token, device starts and the OAuth endpoints (decision M8 #16). The address is the TCP peer, or the rightmost untrusted hop of X-Forwarded-For when the peer is in XENIBASE_TRUSTED_PROXIES (clientIP).
    • Per account. Every wrong password, TOTP code or recovery code, in sign-in, step-up, password change or TOTP setup, goes through recordFailure. The fifth in a row locks the account for 15 minutes, and each further one (after a lock ends) for twice as long as the last, up to a day; only a good sign-in or a new password starts the count again. While locked, every password, the right one included, answers 429 locked with Retry-After. The owner is emailed when a lock starts, at most once an hour (noticeLockout, in the background, so the answer takes no longer). An address with no enabled account is counted the same way in login_address_failures, so it locks after five failures as well, and the lock says nothing about which addresses are registered. A sign-in challenge is also deleted after three wrong codes.
    Resolved

    The lock used to say which addresses had accounts, never grew, and told nobody: five wrong passwords for a registered address answered 429 locked while an unknown one only ever answered 401, the lock was a fixed 15 minutes that reset the count (about 480 TOTP guesses a day for someone with the password), and signup answered an existing address in about 1 ms against 100 ms or more for a new one. Now an address without an enabled account is counted and locked exactly as an account is (login_address_failures, forgotten a day after its last failure), the lock doubles with each failure past the fifth up to a day, as project auth's does (Project auth), the owner is emailed when it starts (at most once an hour), and signup hashes the password and sends one email for an existing address as for a new one (TestLockoutDoublesAndSaysNothing, TestSignupTakesAsLongForAnExistingAddress). Anyone who knows an address can still keep it locked, now for up to a day at a time, within the per-address limit; the email tells the owner, and the right password works once the lock ends.

    Sessions, CSRF and step-up#

    newSession makes 32 random bytes and stores only their SHA-256, with the IP and user agent. Every sign-in makes a new one, so a session cannot be fixed in advance. setSessionCookie sets __Host-xenibase_session with HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict, path / and a 7-day age. The __Host- prefix and Secure are dropped only when XENIBASE_COOKIE_SECURE is false, for plain-HTTP development.

    Authenticate refuses and deletes a session idle for 12 hours, older than 7 days, or whose user is disabled, unapproved or unverified, and touches it at most once a minute (defaults in setDefaults, unchanged by cmd/server). Users list their sessions and revoke any of them. Disabling a user, changing their platform role, resetting their TOTP and resetting their password end all their sessions; changing the password ends all but the current one. Resetting the password or the TOTP also revokes every API token the user has, and changing the password does too unless the request sends revoke_tokens: false.

    CSRF protection is double-submit (checkCSRF). GET /session issues __Host-xenibase_csrf, readable by script, and returns its value. Every mutating request from a cookie session, sign-in included, must echo it in X-CSRF-Token, and an Origin header, when sent, must name this host. Requests with a bearer token skip the check and ignore the cookie. Routes called by programs (the device start and poll, the OAuth token and revoke endpoints, webhooks, the edge) are in csrfExempt.

    Step-up is a recent second check of the password and, when the account has TOTP, a code. Reauthenticate stamps sessions.reauth_at, and RecentlyReauthenticated accepts it for 10 minutes. A new session counts as freshly stepped up. Recovery codes do not work here. The guard requires it on the routes in reauthRequired: deleting a project or an organisation, transfers, regenerating recovery codes, break-glass, suspension, a TOTP reset, OAuth consent, creating an API token, backup keys, residency, role management, removing a node, and money. A platform role change (UpdateUser), approving a device login (ApproveDeviceLogin; denying one needs none) and an in-place restore check it in their handlers.

    For tokens, tokenConfirmed asks instead for a confirm field equal to the target's name. A project transfer spans two organisations, so no token can make one.

    Resets, roles and closing an account#

    RequestPasswordReset emails a one-hour link to an address with an enabled account and answers 202 whatever happens. ResetPassword consumes it, sets the password, marks the address verified, revokes every API token and ends every session, in one transaction; the email says so. TOTP stays, so a reset alone does not pass a second factor. xenibase-server admin can print a reset link when mail does not work (PasswordResetLink).

    Someone who lost their authenticator and codes asks the platform admin, who checks who they are outside Xenibase and runs ResetTOTP: the secret and codes go, sessions end, API tokens are revoked, and the user is emailed.

    SetPlatformRole makes or unmakes platform admins and support staff. From the UI the account must be enabled, approved, verified and have TOTP (ineligible); from the server those checks are skipped, for when nobody is left who can. The last active platform admin cannot be demoted. The change ends the user's sessions and emails them.

    SetDisabled is the closest thing to deleting an account: sessions end at once, and the UserDisabled hook (revokeEverywhere) revokes every API token and drops the user's personal database logins in every organisation. Memberships stay. A platform admin cannot disable themselves.

    Resolved

    Recovering an account used to leave its API tokens, and a session minted them without step-up: ResetPassword, ChangePassword and ResetTOTP deleted only sessions, and neither POST /tokens nor POST /auth/device/approve needed step-up though OAuth consent did (decision OAuth #4), so a stolen cookie could create a 365-day admin token that outlived the owner's reset, and a /device?code=… link was one click from a 90-day token. Now a password reset and a two-factor reset revoke every token the user has, in the same transaction, and their emails say so; a password change does too unless the user unticks Also revoke my API tokens (revoke_tokens, on by default). POST /tokens is in reauthRequired, and approving a device login checks for a recent step-up in its handler; the web UI's step-up dialog answers both (TestRecoveryRevokesTokens, TestTokensNeedARecentStepUp).

    Organisations, members and invitations#

    Every new user gets a personal organisation, "name's projects", on the Personal plan, or Unlimited for the platform admin. Its owner cannot leave it and it cannot be deleted; otherwise it is an ordinary organisation, and others can be invited to it. Any signed-in user can create more (orgs.Create), each on the Personal plan with them as owner, with no limit on how many.

    Membership changes run under a lock on the organisation's members (withMembersLocked), so two requests cannot remove the last owner between them:

    ChangeWhoRules
    Change a role (SetMemberRole)Owners and adminsOnly owners give or take owner or billing. The last owner keeps the role. Becoming billing drops every project membership. Then the user's database logins are set to their new access, or dropped (refreshAccess).
    Remove (RemoveMember)Owners and adminsOnly owners remove owners; never the last. Project memberships and the user's tokens for the organisation go in the same transaction (deleteMembership), then their database logins.
    Leave (Leave)Any member; a token needs writeNot a personal organisation, not the last owner. As removal.
    Transfer ownership (TransferOwnership)An owner, with step-upThe new owner must already be a member; the old one becomes admin.
    Project membership (AddProjectMember)Project adminsThe user must be a member of the organisation and not billing. Removal also removes them from the project's live branches.

    Invite records an invitation (32 random bytes, SHA-256 at rest, 7 days, single use) and emails the link, which the inviter also sees once in case the email does not arrive. An organisation invitation names an organisation role and optional project roles; owners and admins send them (InviteOrgMember keeps owner and billing to owners), and a project admin adding an address that is not yet a member sends one as member with that project role. An organisation invitation is refused for an address that is already a member: roles change with SetMemberRole and projects with AddProjectMember. A platform invitation, the platform admin's, carries no roles and is refused for an address that has an account. Organisation invitations are capped a day per organisation and per inviter (below). Neither checks the signup mode or the domain allow-list: in every mode, an invitation is a way in.

    accept takes a pending, unexpired, unrevoked invitation. An address that has an account must accept it signed in as that account, by link or from the in-app list. An address without one creates the account with the link (CreateVerifiedUser: verified and approved, since the link proves the address) and goes straight on to sign-in (AcceptInvitation). Marking it accepted and adding the memberships share one transaction, and a project that has left the organisation since is skipped.

    Resolved

    An accepted invitation, or a project transfer, used to turn a billing member into a plain member: InsertOrgMember's ON CONFLICT wrote member for anything below admin, and Invite refused an existing member only when no projects were listed, so an admin could take a billing member's billing access away and give them a project, which SetMemberRole keeps to owners. Now the CASE keeps the existing role unless the new one is higher (owner, then admin), Invite refuses any existing member, accept adds no projects for someone who is billing by then, and Transfer takes the project away from a project member who is billing in the destination, with their logins on it (TestBillingIsKept). Billing members demoted this way before the change are not restored.

    Resolved

    Invitations used to be an unlimited mail relay with words the sender chose: nothing counted them, every user owns an organisation, and the organisation's and inviter's names went through linkify, so "Security team https://evil.test/reset" became a link beside the real button. Now checkInvitationLimits allows an organisation 100 invitations in any 24 hours and an inviter 50 across their organisations (XENIBASE_INVITES_PER_ORG_DAY, XENIBASE_INVITES_PER_USER_DAY; 0 turns a cap off), revoked ones included, and answers 429 rate_limited with Retry-After past them. Both names, and the first name in every greeting (mail.Hi), go through mail.Inert, which puts an invisible zero-width space after each ., :, / and @: they read the same but are not made links, here or by most mail clients (TestInvitationsAreCapped, TestInvitationNamesAreNotLinks). Platform invitations, the platform admin's, are not capped.

    A project moves between organisations with POST /projects/{id}/transfer. TransferProject needs step-up and org.owner on both organisations; a destination the caller cannot see answers 404. Transfer refuses a project that is not active, a branch, a parent with live branches, and one with backups on the source's own storage targets. Its project members join the destination as members (one who is billing there stays billing and loses the project), every table carrying the project's org_id follows by ON UPDATE CASCADE, tokens of the old organisation lose the project, and tokens left with no projects are revoked. The destination's plan limits are not checked here.

    An owner deletes an organisation by typing its name (RequestOrgDeletion, step-up). Personal organisations are refused. The organisation is deleting for 7 days, in which only reads and owner-only actions such as cancelling work, then each project gets a final backup and is deleted, and memberships and invitations end.

    authz.Can#

    Every tenant route declares a scope and an action in routeRules. authorize turns the scope into an organisation, a project and a branch's parent, and asks authz.Can. The answer has two parts. Visible false answers 404, so a caller cannot tell a resource they may not see from one that does not exist. Allowed false answers 403.

    ActionLeast roleToken scope
    org.viewAny member, billing includedread
    org.manage, org.auditOrg adminadmin (org.audit: read)
    org.ownerOrg owneradmin
    org.billingOwner or billing, not under break-glassadmin
    org.create_projectOrg admin, or a member when the organisation allows it; never billingwrite
    project.view, .credentials, .console_readProject read_onlyread
    .console_write, .table_edit, .backup, .branch, .automation, auth users, files, realtimeDeveloperwrite (auth users and files reads: read)
    .settings, .services, .members, .promote, .delete, .restore_inplace, .backup_storage, .auditProject adminadmin (.audit: read)
    project.export, .residency, .manage_rolesOrg owner, not under break-glass; visible to read_onlyadmin

    The scopes are in actionScope; an action missing from it needs admin. Org owners and admins are project admins everywhere. A member who is not on a project, and a billing member asking for any project action, gets Visible false. In a suspended organisation only the four actions in readActions work; in a deleting one, those and org.owner, so an owner can cancel.

    For a token, Can first answers 404 for any organisation but the token's, and for a project outside its restriction unless the resource is a branch of a project inside it (Resource.ParentID, V2 §8: a CI token restricted to a project creates and uses its branches). It then decides with the user's current roles, so a token loses what its user loses at once, and last checks the scope: a user who may act but whose token lacks the scope gets 403 insufficient_scope, and a project-restricted token is refused every organisation action but org.view. On scopeSelf routes a token needs the scope in the route's token field, and routes without one are for sessions only. visibleProjects narrows lists the same way.

    Resolved

    A read-scoped token used to be able to make two changes: POST /orgs/{org}/leave is declared as org.view, so a read token could make its user leave, which revokes all their tokens there and drops their database logins; and DELETE /tokens/{token_id} took read, so it could revoke its user's admin tokens. A leaked read-only CI token or a read-only OAuth app could cut its user off. Now LeaveOrg needs the write scope from a token (the route stays org.view, so billing members can still leave), and RevokeMyToken needs it to revoke any token but the caller itself, which xenibase logout does with whatever scope it has (TestReadTokensChangeNothing).

    Platform admins have no tenant role by being platform admins. platform.manage and support.console are session-only and answer 403, not 404. Support staff see the support console and organisations' metadata, never data. Backups and operations with no project are platform work and answer 404 to anyone else. To act inside an organisation they are not in, a platform admin opens a break-glass session (StartBreakGlass): step-up, a reason, 1 minute to 4 hours on the database clock, refused if they are already a member. Every owner is emailed, members see a banner, any owner can end it, and every audited request under it (every mutating one, and the audited reads) writes a row with break_glass set, in the organisation's log and the platform's. It hands out nothing that would outlive it: invitations, organisation and project role changes and ownership transfers answer 403 break_glass (refuseBreakGlass).

    Resolved

    Break-glass could be turned into permanent membership: under it the platform admin is an org admin, could invite their own address as admin, and accept, after which can found a real membership that outlived the session and an owner ending it, with nothing flagged break_glass. Now refuseBreakGlass answers 403 break_glass to invitations (organisation and project), organisation and project role changes, and ownership transfers made under break-glass, and everything else it allows is unchanged. Invite refuses anyone's own address, and accept refuses an invitation sent by the account accepting it, so one sent before the change cannot be used either (TestBreakGlassCannotGrantMembership). A membership already gained this way stays: the organisation's audit log shows the invitation with break_glass set.

    API tokens and device login#

    A token is xb_ and 43 characters drawn uniformly from base62 (newSecret), shown once. Only its SHA-256 and its first 9 characters are kept, the latter for display; a slow hash would add nothing to 256 bits. It has a name, one organisation, scopes (NormalizeScopes: read, write includes read, admin requires write), an optional project list, and an expiry from 1 hour to the platform's maximum (365 days, lowered under Settings), 90 days by default. Creating one emails the user its name, prefix, scopes and expiry (notifyCreated); a week before expiry they are emailed again.

    tokens.Authenticate refuses a token that is revoked, expired, or whose user is disabled, unapproved or unverified, answers 403 for a suspended organisation, and records the last use and IP at most once a minute. tokenSession then applies 600 requests a minute per token and 1,200 per organisation. Users revoke their own tokens (a token with write, or any token revoking itself); org owners and admins see and revoke every token in the organisation. Leaving or being removed revokes the user's tokens there, and disabling the user, resetting their password or their TOTP revokes all of them. A session creates a token only within 10 minutes of a step-up.

    A token may create tokens, unless an OAuth app holds it; the new one records its parent and is revoked with it. checkTokenGrant, used for every new token whatever its source, checks that the user can see the organisation and every listed project, and, when the caller is itself a token, that it was not issued to an app and that the new one has no scope, project or lifetime beyond it:

    The CLI's login is RFC 8628's device flow (StartDevice). POST /auth/device, 60 per 5 minutes per address, returns a 32-byte device code (stored as its SHA-256) and an 8-letter user code from 20 consonants (newUserCode, about 2.6 × 1010 codes), both valid 10 minutes, with read and write requested unless the CLI asks otherwise. The user opens /device?code=… while signed in, sees the client's name and scopes, chooses the organisation, may narrow the scopes and restrict projects, and approves (ApproveDeviceLogin), confirming their password and code first unless they did in the last 10 minutes. ApproveDevice creates the token and seals its secret into the request, bound to the device code's hash, in one transaction. PollDevice answers authorization_pending, slow_down (polls closer than 2.5 seconds), access_denied or expired_token, and hands over the secret once, deleting the request. Looking a user code up needs a session, so codes cannot be tried from outside.

    Third-party OAuth apps#

    An app such as Taskiem asks a user to connect an organisation through RFC 6749's authorization code grant with PKCE (the integrator's guide). What it receives is an ordinary API token, so everything in the section above applies to it.

    1. Register. The platform admin registers a client from a session (CreateClient): a name, 1 to 10 redirect URIs, absolute, https or loopback http, no fragment (ValidateRedirectURI), the most scopes it may ask for (read and write by default), and whether it is confidential. A confidential client gets an xbc_ secret, kept as its SHA-256; a public one relies on PKCE alone.
    2. Consent. The app sends the user to /oauth/authorize. ValidateAuthorize needs a live client, a redirect URI equal to a registered one, state of at most 512 characters, an S256 challenge (plain is refused), and scopes within the client's. A bad request is shown on the page and never redirected. The page needs a session and step-up; its first call also returns the request sealed for the user (consent), which the approval sends back. The user picks the organisation, scopes (within those sealed), projects and expiry, and DecideOAuthAuthorization runs checkTokenGrant, then IssueCode stores a 32-byte code (SHA-256, 10 minutes) with the user's choices and the challenge, and the browser is sent to the redirect URI with code and state. A denial is sent there with error=access_denied.
    3. Exchange. POST /oauth/token, form or JSON, client credentials in the body or HTTP Basic but not both, 60 per 5 minutes per address. Exchange authenticates the client (authenticateClient: a public client must send no secret), locks the code row, and checks that it was issued to this client, is unused and unexpired, has the same redirect URI, and that the verifier's SHA-256 matches the challenge. It creates the token and marks the code used in one transaction. A code presented a second time fails and revokes the token its first use issued. There is no refresh token.
    4. Revoke. The app revokes its own tokens with RFC 7009's endpoint (RevokeByClient), answering 200 for any token. The user disconnects the app from Account; org owners and admins revoke it with the organisation's tokens; the platform admin disabling the client revokes every token it was issued (DisableClient).
    Resolved

    Disconnecting or disabling an app used to leave the tokens it made for itself: an OAuth token with write could call POST /api/v1/tokens, and the child had no oauth_client_id, so DisableClient and Account's Disconnect left it working for up to a year. Now a token created by a token records it in api_tokens.parent_id (migration 00088), and a trigger on revoked_at revokes a token's children, and theirs, in the same statement, whichever path revokes it: Disconnect, the organisation's list, the app's own revocation, a reused code, or disabling the app. And checkTokenGrant refuses an OAuth-issued token any new token (403 token_not_allowed): the app holds exactly what the user consented to (TestRevokingATokenRevokesWhatItMade, TestTokenMadeByATokenGoesWithIt, TestOAuthFlowOverHTTP). Children made before the migration have no recorded parent.

    Platform email#

    One SMTP configuration, set in the setup wizard and under Settings, sends all of Xenibase's own email (mail.Service). The password is sealed with the master key, and PutMailSettings saves a configuration only after a test message gets through. Validate takes STARTTLS on 587 (the default, refused if the server does not offer it), implicit TLS on 465, or none, meant for a relay on the same host but not limited to one; TLS is 1.2 or later. Unlike a project's own SMTP server, the platform's is not put through the outbound rules: the platform admin chooses it. A message is multipart/alternative, plain text first, then HTML in one branded layout (Render); header values have CR and LF replaced, and lines starting with . are dot-stuffed.

    MessageToSent by
    Verify your address; you already have an accountThe signup addressSignup, ResendVerification
    Reset your passwordThe address, if it has an enabled accountRequestPasswordReset
    Approved; two-factor on, off or reset; platform role changed; sign-in locked (at most once an hour)The userauth
    InvitationAny address an inviter entersorgs.Invite
    Token created; token expires in a weekThe token's usertokens
    Break-glass opened; organisation to be deletedEvery ownertenancy

    Account email is sent synchronously in the request, except the lockout notice, which goes in the background so a lock answers as fast as anything else. A failure to send an approval, two-factor or role email is logged and the change stands. A failed invitation email is reported to the inviter with the link. Organisation invitations are capped a day per organisation and per inviter (above); the rest is limited only by the per-address request limiter, in memory and per process, and goes to the account's own address. Names that someone else chose (an organisation's, an inviter's, a token's, the greeting's) go into a message through mail.Inert, so a web address in one is never a link.

    Spec and code#

    Spec and code differ

    V1 §7.2 (V1 7.2), V2 §3.1 (V2 3.1) and V3 §7.4 make TOTP mandatory for every account, enrolled before first use, and V1 makes step-up "password + TOTP". Since the change recorded in the changelog ("Two-factor sign-in is off by default for ordinary accounts"), only platform admins and support staff must have it. Ordinary accounts sign in, and step up, with a password alone until they turn it on.

    Spec and code differ

    V2 §3.6 (V2 3.6) specifies account deletion by the user, blocked while they are the last owner of an organisation with projects, removing memberships, tokens, database logins and an empty personal organisation. There is no such route. Decision M9 #12 defers it, and the terms tell users to ask the platform admin, whose only tool is disabling the account, which keeps the row, the memberships and the personal organisation.

    Spec and code differ

    V3 §7.4 (V3 7.4) opens signup with "one Free org per user", and the acceptable use policy forbids getting around it. Nothing enforces it: orgs.Create makes any number of organisations for any user, each on the Personal quota plan, which is what the Free plan maps to, so the Free tier's limits multiply with the number of organisations a user creates.

    Resolved

    OAuth consent narrows, never widens, the scopes the app asked for (decision OAuth #4). The server used to keep nothing between the page's two calls, and DecideOAuthAuthorization checked the posted scopes only against the client's allowed ones, so the narrowing was the page's alone. Now GET /oauth/authorize returns the validated request sealed with the master key for that user, 30 minutes long (SealConsent); an approval must send it back, and OpenConsent checks the user, client, redirect URI and challenge and supplies the requested scopes, beyond which a posted scope is refused (TestOAuthFlowOverHTTP).

    Failure handling#

    If this happensWhat Xenibase does
    SMTP is not configuredSignup answers 503 mail_not_configured, after creating the account; resend answers 202 without sending; reset requests answer 202 and log; invitations are created and the inviter gets the link with the error
    The SMTP server refuses or is downThe request that sends fails for signup (500 after the account was created, so the user asks for a new link); other account email is logged and the change stands; nothing is retried
    Turnstile cannot be reached or rejects the token400 challenge_failed; the signup is refused
    Too many attempts from one address429 rate_limited with Retry-After: 60; the window is per process, so it resets on restart and is per server
    Five failures in a row on an account, or on an address without one429 locked with Retry-After, for the right password too: 15 minutes, doubling with each further failure up to a day; the owner is emailed
    The master key cannot open a TOTP secret or the recovery codesSign-in fails with a 500 for that account; the platform admin resets its two-factor
    Step-up is older than 10 minutes403 reauth_required; the web client asks and retries
    New terms are published403 terms_required for sessions, except on beforeTerms routes, until the user accepts; tokens are not affected
    An organisation sends its 100th invitation in 24 hours, or an inviter their 50thThe next answers 429 rate_limited with Retry-After until the oldest counted is a day old
    Two accept the same invitation, or it is revoked meanwhileMarkInvitationAccepted updates one row; the other gets 404. Two creating the same address get 409
    Refreshing database logins after a role change failsThe role change stands and the call answers 500; the next change or a credential request brings the login in line
    A device login is approved but never polledThe token exists, its secret sealed in the request; the sweep deletes the request an hour after expiry and the token cannot be collected, but it lives until revoked or expired
    A code is exchanged twice400 invalid_grant and the token from the first exchange is revoked
    An organisation is suspendedIts tokens answer 403 org_suspended; sessions can only read

    Security and tenant isolation

    The shared tier's isolation checklist and its checks, secrets under the master key and their rotation, outbound requests, signatures, quotas and the isolation tests.

    Xenibase runs other people's databases side by side. On the shared tier, many organisations' projects are databases in one Postgres cluster, behind one pair of poolers, reached from one set of servers. This page is the whole of how they are kept apart and how the platform's own secrets are kept: what each kind of attacker can reach, the master key, the isolation checklist and its live audit, the per-tenant limits in tenancy, outbound requests, and the tests. The pieces that belong to one service are on that service's page and are linked from here, not repeated.

    • crypto316 linesXenibase's cryptographic helpers.
    • rotate507 linesRe-encrypts every secret Xenibase stores under the primary master key (spec §7.3: "The master key can be rotated with a CLI command that re-encrypts the stored secrets"), and keeps the derive seed (seed.go) that the derived passwords come from.
    • isocheck910 linesVerifies the shared tier's tenant isolation checklist (spec §7.1) against a live cluster: its configuration, every project on it, and two throwaway tenants that try to reach each other.
    • outbound631 linesThe only way tenants make Xenibase send traffic (webhooks and HTTP jobs, V2 §9.1, §10.7): requests go only to public addresses unless the platform admin allow-listed the host for the organisation, connect to the address that was checked …
    • signature73 linesThe Xenibase-Signature scheme: an HMAC-SHA256 over "<unix time>.<body>", sent as t=<unix>,v1=<hex>.
    • tenancy1,831 linesImplements V2's multi-tenant hardening (§10): quotas and per-org rate limits, storage enforcement, the statement reaper, usage recording, suspension, break-glass, dedicated allowances, and org deletion.

    Who the attackers are#

    V2 assumes any tenant may be careless or hostile (V2 §10.1). A malicious platform admin with root, timing and cache side channels between tenants on one cluster, and network-level denial of service are out of scope. Tenants who need more use a per-organisation shared cluster or a dedicated instance.

    AttackerWhat they holdWhat they can reachWhat stops them going further
    Another tenantAn owner login and SQL of their choosing on a shared cluster; the console, webhooks, jobsTheir own database; the catalogs every role reads (pg_database, pg_roles); any route of the poolers, whose auth file is one namespaceCONNECT for the project's roles only, role attributes, hidden activity, opaque names, the limits and the reaper, the outbound client (below, Connections: poolers and the edge)
    A tenant's end userA publishable key and a user tokenThat project's backend services, as anon or userThe host alone picks the project; keys and tokens are that project's; row-level security (The data API)
    An internet attackerNothingThe poolers, the edge, the web API, the wakerTLS and SCRAM against stored verifiers; IP allowlists; sign-in limits; the PgBouncer console refused from public addresses (Connections: poolers and the edge)
    A compromised node or agentRoot on a machine that runs instancesEvery database on it, and its containers' environment (admin passwords, S3 credentials, the WAL-G key)Nothing on the node; its mTLS certificate is pinned to its node id (Nodes and agents). Accepted in the review
    A compromised edgeIts region's feedEvery project's edge and request-role passwords and active signing keys, so any project's service roleIt never reads the metadata database; the feed is signed per edge (Connections: poolers and the edge)
    A compromised pooler hostPgBouncer's files, the hostname's TLS keyEvery verifier in the region, every session's plaintext, the private networkVerifiers cannot log in, but can pose as the server. Backends use server_tls_sslmode = prefer, so the network is trusted (Connections: poolers and the edge)
    A compromised xenibase-serverThe master key and the metadata owner roleEverything, the audit log includedNothing in the software; break-glass is an audit control (V2 §2.4)

    Secrets under the master key#

    Secrets the control plane must read back are sealed with one 32-byte master key (V1 §7.3). Which columns are sealed, hashed or kept in the clear is on The metadata data model. This section is how the sealing works and what depends on the key.

    The keyring#

    loadMasterKey reads exactly one of XENIBASE_MASTER_KEY or XENIBASE_MASTER_KEY_FILE (for Docker and systemd secrets), as base64 in either alphabet, padded or not, and refuses anything that does not decode to 32 bytes (ParseKey). XENIBASE_MASTER_KEY_PREVIOUS holds old keys, comma-separated. NewKeyring makes the first the primary and indexes all of them by key id. A key id is the first 8 bytes of SHA-256 over a fixed label and the key, so it names the key without revealing it.

    A ciphertext is version (1) | key id (8) | nonce (12) | AES-256-GCM. The version byte and key id are part of the associated data, and so is the caller's context, which names the column and the row ("nodes.pg_admin_secret:" + id). A sealed value copied into another row, or into another column, fails to open with ErrDecrypt. Decrypt picks the key by the id in the header and answers ErrUnknownKey when the keyring does not hold it. The nonce is random for every seal, and no key seals anywhere near 232 values, so nonce reuse is not a concern.

    Values derived from the seed#

    Derive is HMAC-SHA256 over a label, keyed on the derive seed: 32 bytes sealed under the master key in the derive_seed settings row. The server loads it after migrating (rotate.LoadDeriveSeed) and sets it on the keyring before any service has it. The first server to start creates it (deriveSeed, under an advisory lock): on an install that already has projects the seed is the primary key, which is what Derive keyed on before the seed existed, so nothing changes on upgrade; a new install gets random bytes. A keyring without a seed (tests, tools that derive nothing) keys on its primary key. Derive gives values that must be stable and secret without storing them:

    LabelUsed asStored anywhere?
    xenibase edge role <role>The password of each project's edge login and four request roles, handed to the edge in the feed (edgePassword)No. Their SCRAM verifiers are, in project_services.edge_verifier and login_verifiers, and the poolers authenticate against those
    xenibase console role <role>The console logins' password (ConsolePassword)No. A failed login repairs the role and retries once (decision)
    xenibase storage urls <ref>The key that signs a project's file URLs (storageSecret, File storage)No
    pooler admin scram salt:<user>The salt of the PgBouncer admin user's verifier, so the auth file is byte-identical across syncs (setupProvisioning)No

    Rotation and verification#

    xenibase-server -rotate-master-key runs with the new key as primary and the old one in XENIBASE_MASTER_KEY_PREVIOUS, then exits (rotateMasterKey). It migrates the schema, then rotate.Run collects every sealed value under FOR UPDATE in one transaction: the 16 sealed columns, the seven blobs in settings rows (the derive seed among them), and the secrets in pending operations' parameters. Each one not already under the primary key is re-sealed with the same associated data. Sign-in challenges are deleted rather than re-sealed; their owners sign in again.

    Before Run, PrepareDeriveSeed makes the derive seed if no server of this release has made it yet: from the old key, sealed under it, so the rotation re-seals it and a rotation that rolls back leaves a seed the old key opens. With more than one previous key it cannot tell which one the servers derived from, and refuses. A wrong old key, or a value sealed under a key the keyring does not hold, fails the transaction and nothing changes. After the commit, rotate.Verify opens every value again with a keyring that holds the new key alone, and fails if projects exist without a derive seed. TestEveryEncryptIsRotated reads every Encrypt call in the module and fails on associated data the column list does not cover, so a new sealed column cannot be forgotten silently (The metadata data model has the earlier gap this closed).

    Resolved

    Rotating the master key used to take every project's backend services offline. Derive keyed on the primary key, so after a rotation edgePassword returned new passwords and the feed handed them to the edge, while the poolers (PoolerEdgeUsers) and the instances kept the verifiers stored at enable time, which ensureRolesOn reuses; every data API, auth, storage and realtime request failed SCRAM until the verifiers were cleared by hand, and signed file URLs stopped verifying. Derive now keys on the sealed derive seed, which a rotation re-seals and never replaces, so the edge and request roles' passwords, the console passwords, the file URL keys and the pooler admin's salt are the same before and after. TestMasterKeyRotation turns backend services on and checks that a keyring with the new key alone and the reloaded seed derives passwords that still match the stored verifiers; TestDerivedSurviveRotation compares the services' derived values across a rotation.

    Running servers during a rotation

    The operations guide stops the bundle's one server first. With several, one still running on the old key alone cannot open re-sealed values and keeps sealing new ones under the old key, which are lost once it is dropped. Stop every server, and keep the old key in XENIBASE_MASTER_KEY_PREVIOUS until a second rotation rewraps nothing. The derived passwords are not at stake: a server holds the derive seed it loaded at startup, and the seed's value does not change.

    What is lost with the key#

    Everything sealed: storage credentials, the agent and etcd CA keys, instance admin and Patroni passwords, projects' JWT signing keys and backup keys, webhook secrets, jobs, auth providers' settings, and the platform backup key. Project passwords are not affected, since only their verifiers exist. Backups survive only through the backup key the setup wizard makes the operator download (Backups, restores and imports). The derive seed is sealed too, so the derived values go with the key, and a server without it does not start; a rotation keeps them.

    The shared-tier isolation checklist#

    V1 §7.1 lists what every create enforces; V2 §10.2 and §10.4 add opaque names, activity privacy and the limits a tenant cannot lift. isocheck checks them against live clusters with the same code CI runs. Every check uses a superuser connection to the instance, not the poolers.

    ItemEnforced byChecked by
    CONNECT and TEMPORARY revoked from PUBLIC; granted to the project's own roles onlyensureDatabase; the database is created from template0Roles (every project: every grantee in aclexplode(datacl), databaseGrants); Cluster for postgres and template1
    CREATE on public revoked; the schema owned by the projecthardenDatabaseDatabase
    No SUPERUSER, CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, REPLICATION, BYPASSRLSensureRole spells every attribute outRoles: the owner, <db>_console, <db>_console_ro, <db>_ro, every <db>_u_… and the five backend-service logins (only _service may have BYPASSRLS)
    No membership of pg_* or privileged roles; member logins hold only their own project's roles; the read-only console login cannot become the owner; the backend-service logins hold no role at allNever granted; ensureRolesOn revokes the edge's old membershipsRoles
    A connection limit and a temp_file_limit on every loginensureRole, tempFileLimitRoles (login roles only, the backend-service logins among them)
    A suspended or hard-locked project's logins are offSetLoginsRoles, from Tenant.LoginsOff
    No untrusted language, no plpython3u, plperlu, dblink, postgres_fdw, file_fdw, adminpackTenants cannot create them; the extension API keeps to the allow-listDatabase (EscapeProne)
    No SECURITY DEFINER function owned by anything but the tenant's roles (V2 §10.4)Xenibase's own, in xb_* and xenibase, pin search_pathDatabase (securityDefiners)
    Other sessions' and databases' activity hiddenRestrictActivityDatabase, against ActivityFunctions
    pg_hba.conf: SCRAM, named addresses, hostssl outside private rangesThe bundle's file; xenibase-hba.sh at initdbCluster via pg_hba_file_rules (hbaFinding)
    log_statement = none; only log_min_duration_statementCluster configurationCluster
    Only opaque names in pg_database and pg_rolesOpaque naming (The life of a project)Metadata, from inside a tenant's session

    The live two-tenant probes#

    After auditing every project, Instance drops any leftover probes, creates two throwaway tenants with the real create steps (NewProbe: role, database, hardening), audits their roles, and has A attack B (Probes). B creates a table and keeps a session open. A then tries to connect to B's database, postgres and template1, and runs each of these, every one of which must be refused:

    Among them A tries to grant itself CONNECT on B's database. Then A must fail to read pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_get_activity, pg_stat_database(_conflicts), the per-database and per-backend statistics functions, pg_locks, pg_lock_status(), pg_blocking_pids and pg_prepared_xacts, to raise its temp_file_limit or connection limit, and must not be a member of any predefined role. A success is a finding. An error counts as a refusal only if its SQLSTATE class is one Postgres uses for refusals (isRefusal); any other error fails the run, so a broken probe cannot pass for a refused one. The probes are dropped afterwards, even when the run fails.

    How often, and the alert#

    Due runs every hour and queues an isolation_check operation for each running shared cluster whose latest check is older than Every (24 hours) and not queued or running. A check has two attempts and 30 minutes. Any finding fails it permanently, with the first three findings in the error and all of them in the step log. A failed check of a cluster that still exists raises the critical isolation_check_failed alert (alerts), which clears when a later check succeeds. Platform admins can run all checks at once from Settings → Tenant isolation (POST /api/v1/security/isolation-checks).

    Resolved

    The audit used to pass while the backend-service logins, or a cross-project grant, were wrong. Roles never looked at the five backend-service logins, which tenant SQL runs as on the shared tier, so a request role left with LOGIN while its organisation was suspended, without temp_file_limit or a connection limit, with an unexpected attribute or a predefined role passed; and the grants check asked only whether PUBLIC had CONNECT, so CONNECT on B's database granted to A's owner passed too. Now Roles checks the five logins' attributes (BYPASSRLS on _service alone), limits, NOLOGIN while suspended or hard-locked, and requires them to hold no role; and databaseGrants reads every grantee of CONNECT and TEMPORARY from aclexplode(datacl) and reports any that is not the project's own (or the owner, a superuser, or a move's login). TestRolesServiceLoginsAndGrants breaks each on the test cluster; TestLiveIsolationCheck turns a project's backend services on and breaks them through the operation, and the live probes try the grant.

    Resolved

    V2 §10.4's audit of forbidden capabilities includes "no SECURITY DEFINER functions owned by anything other than tenant roles or the fixed Xenibase webhook function" (V2 §10.4), and isocheck used to never read prosecdef. Database now reports a SECURITY DEFINER function owned by a superuser or a role not of that database, other than an extension's, unless it is one of Xenibase's own in an xb_* schema or xenibase (the backend services' functions, The data API, and the webhook trigger) with its search_path set (TestSecurityDefiners).

    Resolved

    The package comment of isocheck, the doc comments of TestClusterConfiguration and TestLiveIsolationCheck, and the security review used to say the live check runs weekly (and nightly in places). They now say every 24 hours, which is Every, as V2 §10.4 asks; V1 §7.1 said weekly.

    Postgres-level hardening#

    The checklist is the minimum. These are the settings behind it and what each one stops:

    ControlWhereWhat it stops
    The owner: NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOREPLICATION NOBYPASSRLS INHERIT, CONNECTION LIMIT from the plan, the SCRAM verifier as its passwordensureRoleTaking any other role or database; creating extra logins to get round the connection limit. CREATEROLE only on a dedicated instance with role management on (The control plane)
    Console and request-role logins: NOINHERIT, reaching the project's roles only by SET ROLE or as themselves; only _service has BYPASSRLSThe control plane, The data APIRESET ROLE in tenant code landing on a superuser or the edge login
    temp_file_limit = 2GB per login, set with ALTER ROLE … SETTempFileLimitOne sort or hash filling the disk. It is superuser-only, so SET and ALTER ROLE … RESET fail for the tenant
    statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout as role defaultsensureRoleNothing on their own: both are user-settable. The reaper is the guard
    The activity views and statistics functions, pg_locks, pg_prepared_xacts and the lock functions behind them revoked from PUBLIC in every shared project databaseRestrictActivity (also run by apply_settings)Seeing other databases' backends, roles, commits, rows and locks
    Platform functions in tenant databases: SECURITY DEFINER only with SET search_path = pg_catalog, pg_temp, in schemas PUBLIC cannot useDatabase webhooks and scheduled jobs, The data APIA tenant's object on the search path running inside a platform function
    Resolved

    pg_locks used to show every backend's database to every tenant. The activity restriction hid which databases had backends, but pg_locks (over pg_lock_status()) stayed readable by PUBLIC and listed every lock in the cluster with its database, relation, mode and pid, so joined with pg_database a tenant saw which other projects were active, with how many sessions, and which relations they touched. Now activityPrivacy also revokes SELECT on pg_locks and pg_prepared_xacts, and ActivityFunctions takes in pg_lock_status, pg_blocking_pids, pg_safe_snapshot_blocking_pids, pg_isolation_test_session_is_blocked and pg_prepared_xact by name, so each major's signatures are covered. isocheck.Database checks them (ActivityViews) and the probes try them. Existing databases get it from apply_settings, which migration 00090 queues for each active shared project, as 00066 did. Query insights' locks view reads as the admin and is unchanged. TestActivityPrivacy covers it on the test cluster.

    Extensions on the shared tier#

    The shared tier allows SharedExtensions: pgcrypto, uuid-ossp, citext, pg_trgm, hstore, unaccent, btree_gin, btree_gist, pg_stat_statements, vector and hypopg. Dedicated instances add postgis, pg_partman, timescaledb, postgres_fdw and pg_cron (V1 §7.4). The rule is that nothing on the shared tier reaches outside its database: no foreign-data wrappers or dblink (they connect from the cluster's own address, which pg_hba.conf trusts), no file access, no background workers running tenant SQL (pg_cron), and no preload library that is unsafe to share. hypopg serves query insights; pg_stat_statements is preloaded cluster-wide, its reset withheld from the request roles (The data API).

    EnableExtension refuses a name outside the tier's list or missing from the image, then creates it as the superuser WITH SCHEMA public. The image (deploy/images/postgres) has every contrib module and hypopg, but not vector.

    The allow-list binds the API, not the tenant

    The owner role owns its database, so it can CREATE EXTENSION any extension Postgres marks trusted without the API: tablefunc, ltree, intarray, fuzzystrmatch and the other trusted contrib modules (checked on Postgres 16). Trusted extensions are by definition ones a non-superuser may install, so none of them escapes the role, and the untrusted ones stay refused. The security review says so: the allow-list binds what Xenibase installs, not what is installed.

    Per-tenant controls#

    tenancy is V2 §10's hardening. Its loops run in every server: the reaper every 15 seconds, storage enforcement every minute, and a sweep every 5 minutes (opaque renames, usage, break-glass expiry, organisation deletion, retention). Each step is idempotent, so several servers converge.

    Quotas and rate limits#

    An organisation's limits are its plan's, with per-org overrides (Limits). A refused create answers 409 quota_exceeded with the limit, the use and the maximum (QuotaError).

    LimitCheckedHow
    Projects, branchesBefore a create, a branch, a restore or import into a new project, a replicaA count (CheckCreateProject, CheckCreateBranch), also refusing an organisation that is not active or has an overdue balance; counted again under the organisation's row lock in the transaction that records the project (claim), and when a branch is detached
    Per-project and total shared storageA branch, a demotionfitsShared against the measured size; continuously by storage enforcement
    Operations in flightBackups, restores, imports, branches, exportsA count of queued and running operations of those kinds
    Backup storage on platform targetsEach backupThe organisation's backups there; its own targets never count
    Connections per projectProvisioningThe role's CONNECTION LIMIT and PgBouncer's max_db_connections
    Concurrent console queriesEach console, editor or table queryAcquireConsole, a counter in the serving process
    API tokensEach bearer request600 a minute per token, 1,200 per organisation, in each server's memory (DefaultTokenRate)

    Webhook and HTTP job limits are on Database webhooks and scheduled jobs; the edge's per-IP, per-key and monthly limits on The data API.

    Resolved

    Parallel creates used to go past the projects quota and the dedicated allowance. CheckCreateProject counted the organisation's projects and the handler then called provision.Create with no lock or recount between the two, so N requests sent at once each saw the same count and all succeeded; CheckCreateBranch, branch detach and WithinAllowance had the same shape, and read replicas were not counted in the allowance at all. Now provision.Create, branching.Detach, dedicated.Promote and CreateReplica call Claim in the transaction that records what they create; tenancy's claim takes the organisation's row (SELECT … FOR UPDATE, LockOrgForQuota) and counts again, so each create sees the ones committed before it, and a late one answers 409 quota_exceeded. TestParallelCreatesKeepTheQuota and TestParallelClaimsKeepTheAllowance send them at once.

    Spec and code differ

    V2 §10.3 says rate limits on console queries and operations are per-org token buckets in xenibase-server. Console queries are a concurrency count per process, so with N servers an organisation gets N times its limit; operations are a count of what is queued or running. Token limits are also per process.

    Storage enforcement and locks#

    Postgres has no per-database disk quota, so EnforceStorage applies one from each shared project's latest measured size (sampled every 5 minutes, ignored if older than 30). A project already at the warning or the soft lock is measured again on every pass with pg_database_size, one admin connection per cluster (liveSizes), since the soft lock lets its tenant keep writing. The ratio is the larger of the project's size against its per-project limit and the organisation's total against its shared-storage limit.

    applyStorageState moves a project between states and records the new state only after it took effect, so a crash part-way repeats the move instead of believing it done. Locks are re-applied every minute.

    • Soft lock. ALTER DATABASE … SET default_transaction_read_only = on, and idle sessions are ended so reconnecting clients pick it up (SetReadOnly). It is a default: a tenant can still open a read-write transaction to delete data, as V2 §10.4 intends, and the database's owner can reset it, which the next pass undoes.
    • Hard lock. At 120%, or when a soft-locked project has grown by 5% of its limit since the server first found it over the limit (grewWhileSoft, a baseline in memory, so a restart starts it again). Every login of the project becomes NOLOGIN, and their sessions end on the poolers and the server (SetLogins). The console logins are left out, so the team can still delete data and run Reclaim space.
    • Unlock. Under 100% the locks lift and the admins are emailed. A hard lock holds until then: a project brought back under 120% stays hard-locked.
    Resolved

    One tenant used to be able to fill a shared node's disk. The hard limit came only from the 5-minute size sample, and the soft lock lets a tenant open a read-write transaction, so a tenant at 99% could insert at disk speed for up to six minutes, tens of gigabytes past a 512 MB limit. Now every enforcement pass (each minute) measures the projects in warn or soft with pg_database_size, so one that reaches 120% is hard-locked within a minute, and a soft-locked project that keeps growing (5% of its limit) is hard-locked without waiting for it to reach 120%. A hard lock lifts only under the limit, so a project is not let back in at 119% to write again. The overshoot is bounded by a minute of writes. TestSoftLockedGrowthIsHardLocked grows a soft-locked database on the test cluster with no new sample and requires the hard lock.

    Spec and code differ

    V2 §10.4 and §10.8 say a hard lock and a suspension revoke CONNECT from the project's login roles. The code sets NOLOGIN on them instead, which also covers routes the poolers keep, and leaves the console logins able to connect.

    The statement reaper#

    statement_timeout is user-settable, so it cannot be the guard. Every 15 seconds Reap connects to each shared cluster as its admin and looks at the client backends in its project databases, other than its own:

    A long statement is cancelled with pg_cancel_backend; a session idle in a transaction is ended with pg_terminate_backend. A statement the reaper already cancelled that is still running, the same backend with the same query_start, caught the cancel, and is ended with its session (statement_terminated); the check reads reaped_sessions, which keeps each cancel's pid and started_at, so a pass on any server counts. Each one acted on is recorded in reaped_sessions with the first 1,000 characters of its query (kept 30 days, The metadata data model) and shown in the project's activity view. Durations are measured against the service clock. Dedicated instances are exempt. The admin's own sessions are excluded; Xenibase's other logins in a project database (the console, restores, moves) are not.

    Resolved

    A statement that caught the cancel used to run for ever. PL/pgSQL can trap query_canceled, so a block such as DO $$ BEGIN LOOP BEGIN PERFORM pg_sleep(600); EXCEPTION WHEN query_canceled THEN NULL; END; END LOOP; END $$ resumed after the reaper's pg_cancel_backend with its query_start unchanged; every 15 seconds the reaper cancelled it again, recorded another row and reported success, and the session never ended. Now each cancel records the backend's pid and the statement's query_start (migration 00089), and reapInstance terminates a backend it finds still running a statement it cancelled (ReapedStatementCancelled), so such a statement lives one pass past the limit at most. TestReaperEndsStatementThatCatchesCancel runs that block on the test cluster and requires a cancel, then a termination.

    Usage recording#

    RecordUsage records every completed hour since a watermark under an advisory lock, one server at a time, and redoes the last recorded hour because points can land late. Rows are upserted, so a repeated run changes nothing, and carry the organisation's plan at the time. Hourly rows roll up to daily after 90 days. The metrics and how they are priced are on Billing, Free tier and capacity.

    Suspension#

    Suspend takes a reason of up to 1,000 characters, takes a final backup of each active project while it still answers, marks the organisation suspended, then switches its logins off (setOrgLogins) and emails the owners. Reinstate reverses it, and also cancels a pending deletion.

    SurfaceWhile the organisation is suspendedWhere
    Postgres loginsThe owner, the V1 owner, members' logins, the logins a dedicated project's owner created (project_owned_logins) and the five backend-service logins become NOLOGIN; their sessions endSetLogins, ProjectLogins
    PoolersThe databases' clients are killed, and the next sync leaves the organisation's routes outPoolerRoutes (Connections: poolers and the edge)
    EdgeRequests answer project_suspended; open WebSockets closeRealtime
    Web API and tokensMembers can sign in and view; mutating calls answer org_suspended; API tokens are refusedThe control plane
    Webhooks, jobs, outboundEvents queue in the outbox; job runs are skipped; outbound.Gate refusesDatabase webhooks and scheduled jobs
    Backups, branch expiryScheduled backups and branch expiry pauseBackups, restores and imports, Database branches
    Dedicated instancesKeep running, with the logins above off—
    Resolved

    Suspension used to leave the logins a dedicated project's owner created able to log in. With role management on, the owner's migrations create logins of their own (such as an app login), recorded in project_owned_logins; ProjectLogins listed the owner, the V1 owner, project_db_users and the service roles but not those, so SetLogins left them LOGIN and their sessions open, reachable at the instance from the private network. Now ProjectLogins includes them, so a suspension or a hard lock switches them off and ends their sessions, and switching back on restores them. The role sync (SyncOwnedRoles) keeps a recorded login it finds NOLOGIN while the project's logins are off, which it would otherwise drop as no longer a login, so reinstating finds it. TestSetLoginsCoversOwnedLogins and TestSyncOwnedRolesKeepsLoginsSwitchedOff cover it.

    Break-glass, dedicated allowances, deletion#

    • Break-glass. StartBreakGlass lets a platform admin who is not a member act as an org admin for 1 minute to 4 hours, with a reason. The expiry is the database's clock, as the authorisation check reads it; every owner is emailed at once, any owner can end it, and actions are flagged in both audit logs.
    • Dedicated allowance. WithinAllowance and WithinAllowanceChange compare the organisation's instances, vCPU, memory and disk in use plus the request against its allowance; in use counts its dedicated projects' instances, a demotion's stopped instance, a queued promotion's target and its read replicas, each the size of its primary (OrgDedicatedUse). Beyond it, a promotion becomes a request the platform admin approves (V2 §10.6). A dedicated create, a promotion and a replica check it again under the organisation's row lock as they are recorded (claim); an approved request skips it. The Unlimited plan skips the check.
    • Organisation deletion. RequestOrgDeletion needs the name typed, refuses a personal organisation, switches logins off at once, and sets a 7-day grace period. FinishOrgDeletions then deletes each project (each with a final backup), and once none is left, in one transaction, keeps final backups for 30 days and removes invitations and memberships.

    Outbound requests and signatures#

    Webhooks, HTTP jobs, a project's own SMTP server and SMS provider, and import sources are the only ways a tenant makes Xenibase open a connection. All of them go through outbound. Database webhooks and scheduled jobs follows a delivery through it; the rules are these:

    DestinationWebhooks, jobs, SMTP, SMS (Check)Database sources (CheckSource)
    Public addressAllowed, https:// onlyAllowed
    RFC 1918, CGNAT, loopback, unique local, multicast, other special rangesOnly if the platform admin allow-listed the host for the organisation; then http:// tooPrivate ranges only if allow-listed; loopback never
    Link-local and metadata (169.254.0.0/16, fe80::/10, fd00:ec2::254)NeverNever
    Xenibase's own nodes, instances and networksLike any address of their kindNever, even allow-listed (PlatformAddrs, Internal)

    Every resolved address must pass, after canon maps IPv4-mapped, NAT64 and 6to4 addresses to the IPv4 they embed. The connection is pinned to the checked address, without proxies or redirects. Gate refuses a suspended organisation or one with outbound traffic off. Requests are counted per organisation, host and day, and the counts swept after 30 days (V2 §10.7).

    The signature is signature: Xenibase-Signature: t=<unix>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of "t.body">, one v1 per secret during a rotation's overlap. Verify refuses a timestamp outside the receiver's tolerance and compares in constant time. The package has no dependencies, so xenibase-status uses it for the server's pushes too. The edge's feed uses its own scheme over method, URI and body (Connections: poolers and the edge).

    The isolation tests and the security review#

    TestTenantIsolation creates two projects through the API, has B keep a table and a schema, and runs A through the probes above and more, through both poolers and directly: B's role with A's password, B's objects by name, pageinspect and pg_buffercache, and the timeouts it starts with. TestClusterConfiguration runs isocheck.Cluster. TestLiveIsolationCheck runs the operation through the API with a project's backend services on, breaks sixteen checklist items one at a time (three of them on the backend-service logins, a grant to another project and a superuser's SECURITY DEFINER function among them), then switches a suspended project's owner and one of its request roles back on, and requires a finding for each. The suite runs in CI on every push; the live check covers production.

    docs/security-review.md maps each item of V1 §7 and the V2, V3 and V4 surfaces to its code and tests, with the findings of each review. Against this commit it is current.

    Resolved

    The review used to differ from the code in six places: it said rotation re-encrypted everything while the derived passwords and URL keys changed; that the live check ran nightly (at the top) and weekly (in the sign-off), where it runs every 24 hours; that isocheck.Roles checked the project's roles, without the backend-service logins and with only PUBLIC's database grants; that the reaper "ends long statements", where it only cancelled them; that the extension allow-list was enforced by the API, which binds only the API's own creates; and that activity was hidden while pg_locks was readable. The code changes above closed four of them, and the review now says what the code does in all six, including the derive seed, the frequency, the service logins and every database grant, the reaper's termination, the trusted extensions a tenant can create itself, and pg_locks.

    Failure handling#

    What failsWhat happens
    The master key is missing, or not 32 bytes of base64The server refuses to start, naming the variable.
    A sealed value was sealed under a key the keyring does not holdErrUnknownKey wherever it is read. A rotation fails with the kind of secret and a hint about XENIBASE_MASTER_KEY_PREVIOUS, and rolls back.
    Rotation's verify step fails after the commitThe command exits with an error naming the secret; the old key is still needed, so keep it in XENIBASE_MASTER_KEY_PREVIOUS.
    An isolation findingThe check fails permanently, with every finding in its log, and the critical isolation_check_failed alert fires until a later check passes.
    The check cannot connect, or a probe returns an error that is not a refusalThe operation fails after two attempts and raises the same alert. The probe tenants are dropped in a deferred call; leftovers are dropped at the next run's start.
    A shared cluster is not runningIt is not checked, and no alert says so.
    A size sample is missing for 30 minutesA project in warn or soft is measured directly; any other is skipped by storage enforcement, and its state stays as it was.
    A cluster cannot be reached to measure its locked projectsThe pass reports the error and uses their samples.
    A storage lock cannot be applied (instance down)The state is not recorded, so the next pass tries again.
    A reaper cancel fails, or one cluster cannot be reachedLogged; the other clusters are still reaped, and the next pass in 15 seconds tries again.
    Suspension's final backup failsLogged as a warning; the suspension goes ahead.
    Switching an organisation's logins fails on one instanceSuspend returns the error after the organisation is marked suspended; its routes are still removed, and isocheck reports a shared project whose logins remain on.
    An outbound destination resolves to a refused address at send timeThe request is not sent; a webhook delivery dead-letters at once (Database webhooks and scheduled jobs).
