    Part F · Running it

    The engineering system

    How the code is checked and shipped: CI, the test suites in test/, generated code, the docs site, the SDKs and the CLI, and the brand in code.

    Checked against ef67bfb · 2026-10-29No changes to its code since

    Xenibase is checked by one GitHub Actions workflow with seven jobs, built by one Makefile, and shipped as a GitHub release built from the tag. Most of the confidence comes from suites that run the real thing: a control plane in-process against real Postgres and PgBouncer, the install bundle in a browser, the install guide as a script. This page lists each check, what it proves and where it stops, and the CLI, SDKs, docs site and brand that the same system builds.

    • docsite379 linesBuilds the documentation site (V4 §8, M36): every Markdown file under docs/ rendered to HTML with the site's navigation, a search index, and links between pages checked.
    • cli6,026 linesThe xenibase command-line tool (V2 §7.1): contexts, device login, and commands for organisations, projects, branches, SQL, backups, promotion, members, tokens and operations, over the generated API client.
    • brand39 linesXenibase's colours and logo paths in one place for the server's own output (email, documents).

    The workflows#

    There are 4 workflow files in .github/workflows. Only one runs by itself on every change.

    WorkflowRuns onPermissions and secretsWhat it does
    ci.ymlEvery push (any branch or tag), every pull_request, Mondays 03:17 UTC, and by handcontents: read. No secrets.Seven jobs, below.
    release.ymlA pushed tag matching v*contents: write, the job's own GITHUB_TOKENBuilds the release artefacts and publishes a GitHub release (The engineering system).
    deploy.ymlBy hand, with a tagcontents: read, checks: read; the production environment's DEPLOY_SSH_KEY and DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTSRefuses a tag whose CI is not green, waits for the environment's reviewers, then runs upgrade on the control server over SSH. concurrency: deploy-production keeps two deploys apart.
    move-20gb.ymlBy hand, on a runner the caller namescontents: readM18's move under writes at full size (20 GB by default), after checking the runner has three times that free.

    The jobs in ci.yml#

    JobWhenWhat it runsWhat a pass proves
    ciAlwaysgolangci-lint; make test-go with a postgres:18 service; test-deploy, test-acmedns, test-web, test-sdk, docs-site, check-generated, build, release-check; then test-integration (with a 1 GB move) and test-acmeLint is clean; unit and database tests pass under -race; docs links resolve; generated code is current; the binaries are static and embed the real UI; the integration, isolation and SDK live suites pass against real Postgres 18 and PgBouncer; a certificate can be had over HTTP-01.
    e2eAlwaysmake test-e2e: the compose bundle with Pebble, a fake S3 and a Supabase-shaped source, driven by PlaywrightA fresh install reaches a working database through the browser, and the 20 journeys after it work end to end.
    docs-installAlwaysmake test-docsThe commands in docs/install.md, run as written in a clean clone, produce an install that passes the first browser journey.
    atlasAlways; the second step on pull requests onlynode docs/atlas/atlas.mjs check, then a diff against the base branchEvery reference in this atlas resolves, and a pull request that changed its pages also rebuilt site/index.html (How the atlas is maintained).
    upgradeWeekly, by hand, on tags, and on branches named feat/deploy…make test-upgrade (90-minute limit)The previous release installs, a release with a broken migration is rolled back with its data, and an upgrade to this commit comes up at the new version and schema.
    auditAlwaysgovulncheck@v1.1.4 on the module and sdk/go; npm audit --audit-level=high in web, test/e2e and sdk/jsNo known vulnerability in Go code that is actually called, and none rated high or critical in the three npm trees.
    loadWeekly and by hand onlymake test-load with pgbench run from the postgres:18 image; uploads tmp/load-report.md150 shared projects with pgbench on 10, the V2 and backend-services load, realtime load and billing rating at 1,000 organisations stay within their limits.

    The ci job is one long sequence on one runner. Its order matters: the Postgres-backed unit tests run first against the service container on port 5432; the dev compose environment for the integration suite comes up last, on its own ports, so the two never meet. On failure it prints the dev environment's logs and the failing lines of the integration log. The integration step pipes through tee under set -o pipefail, so the tee does not hide a failure.

    ci.yml sets no concurrency and triggers on both push and pull_request, so a branch with an open pull request runs every job twice and a newer push does not cancel an older one: runner time, not correctness. There is no pull_request_target anywhere: pull requests from forks get a read-only token and no secrets.

    Actions and pinning#

    The actions/* actions are pinned to major tags (@v4, @v5) everywhere except the atlas job, which pins checkout and setup-node to commit SHAs. The two third-party actions, golangci/golangci-lint-action@v8 (linter v2.14) and dart-lang/setup-dart@v1 (SDK 3.9.4), are pinned to major tags too.

    They run in the ci job, which has a read-only token and no secrets, so a moved tag could break or falsify that job but could not publish or deploy. The release job, which can write, uses only actions/*; the deploy job, which holds the SSH key, uses none and connects with StrictHostKeyChecking yes. The tag input reaches the shell only through an environment variable and is checked against ^v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+([.-][A-Za-z0-9.]+)?$ and then by git rev-parse, so it cannot carry shell syntax.

    The deploy gate reads the check runs on the tag's commit. Nothing may be failed, cancelled, timed out or pending, and four jobs must have passed by name:

    The Makefile#

    Makefile is the only entry point CI uses; every CI step is a make target, so a contributor can run the same thing locally. It runs recipes under bash -eu -o pipefail, and exports GOFLAGS += -tags=nodynamic (why: without it the image codecs load libwebp through purego and xenibase-server and xenibase-edge become dynamically linked).

    TargetWhat it does
    dev-up, dev, run-dev, dev-downThe dev environment (deploy/dev/compose.yaml: metadata and shared Postgres, two PgBouncers), then the server under air with Vite, or the built binary. A throwaway master key goes to tmp/dev-master.key at mode 600.
    generate, check-generatedRegenerate sqlc, oapi-codegen and openapi-typescript output; fail if that changed a tracked file.
    build, release-check, releaseThe UI, then five static binaries in bin/ with the version linked in; the real UI and no purego; the release artefacts in dist/.
    test-go, test-web, test-db, test-sdkgo test -race ./...; the UI's tsc -b and Vitest; the Go tests against the dev environment; the SDKs' unit tests.
    test-integrationBuilds the agent binary, the Postgres 17 and 18 images, the pooler host and status images, starts the test profile, sources deploy/dev/test.env, and runs go test -race -count=1 -p 1 -timeout 60m ./test/....
    test-e2e, test-docs, test-upgrade, test-deploy, test-acmedns, test-acmeThe suites below.
    test-load, test-move, test-payments-sandboxLoad, the full-size move, the wallet provider's real sandbox. None runs on a push.
    docs-site, atlas, lintThe docs site into dist/docs; this atlas; golangci-lint run ./....

    The test suites#

    SuiteSizeWhat it needsIn CI
    Package tests in internal/* and cmd/*236 test files at the verified commit; 77 of them reach PostgresXENIBASE_TEST_DATABASE_URL for the database tests; they skip without itci, under -race
    test/integration84 filesThe dev environment's test profile and every variable in test.envci
    test/isolation4 testsAs integrationci, in the same go test run
    test/load5 files, plus TestRatingLoad in internal/billingXENIBASE_TEST_LOAD=1, the load profile, pgbenchload, weekly
    test/e2e20 Playwright tests in one serial fileThe install bundle plus an overlay: Pebble and a DNS stub, a fake S3, SMTP and webhook receivers, a Supabase sourcee2e
    test/docsOne script, then the first e2e testDocker; the overlaydocs-install
    test/upgradeOne scriptThe tags (fetch-depth: 0), Dockerupgrade
    test/deployTwo shell suitesgit and sh; a fake docker that keeps state in filesci
    test/acmednsOne test, its own Go moduleCaddy v2.10.0 and caddy-dns/acmedns v0.7.0, fetchedci
    TestACMEWithPebbleOne testPebble built from source at v2.10.1ci (make test-acme)
    test/sandboxTwo filesXENIBASE_TEST_SANDBOX=1 and the provider's sandbox credentialsNever; by hand
    UI (web/src/**/*.test.ts*)20 files at the verified commitNodeci (make test-web)

    How tests get a database#

    A package test that needs Postgres calls storetest.New. It connects to XENIBASE_TEST_DATABASE_URL, creates xenibase_test_ plus twelve random hex characters, runs every migration, and drops the database with WITH (FORCE) when the test ends. Without the variable the test skips. In CI the variable points at the job's postgres:18 service as its superuser, so these tests always run there.

    The integration and isolation suites go further. testenv.Start builds a complete xenibase-server in-process (API, workers, provisioning and the services, with fakes for S3, SMTP, phone providers, Hetzner and the wallet provider) on a fresh metadata database, and registers the dev environment's shared cluster and test pooler pair. The suites share one pooler pair, which is why they run with -p 1. Each one checks its environment first:

    The skip is what lets make test-go compile and pass over ./test/... without the dev environment, and it is also why a variable missing from test.env turns a suite off without failing it.

    Risk

    Some tests never run in CI, and skips are silent. TestDumpRestoreCopy (the agent's real pg_dump and pg_restore) needs XENIBASE_TEST_PG_BIN, and docker.TestAgainstDaemon needs XENIBASE_TEST_DOCKER. Neither variable is set by the Makefile, test.env or any workflow, so both always skip. The second half of TestDedicatedResize (a size the node cannot hold moves the project) skips when the test node reports fewer than three CPUs, which on a two-core runner (GitHub's standard runner for private repositories) is every run. CI runs go test without -v and does not count skips, so a green run does not say any of this happened. The integration suite covers dumps and restores through the agent, so the first two are a smaller gap than they look; the resize-by-move path has no other test. Fix: set the two variables in the ci job (the dev agent image has the Postgres tools), make the CPU check fail rather than skip when CI is set, and print a skip count from go test -json.

    What the integration suite covers#

    The files are named for what they prove, from provisioning, backups, imports, promotion under a live writer, HA, moves (one under load, at 1 GB in CI) and branches to billing, regions, failure injection (failure_test.go, chaos_test.go), the backend services through a real edge, and the CLI. TestSDKs runs each SDK's live test against a project on a real edge (below). Waiting is done by polling with a deadline (waitFor) rather than by fixed sleeps, though fixed sleeps remain in places.

    The isolation suite is the tenant-escape list from V1 §7.1. TestLiveIsolationCheck runs the same internal/isocheck that xenibase-server runs weekly per shared cluster, so CI and production share one implementation (decision M7 #5).

    The browser journey and the install tests#

    make test-e2e builds the server, agent, Pebble and fake-S3 images and the Postgres images, starts the bundle from deploy/compose/compose.yaml with compose.e2e.yaml over it, and runs Playwright with Chromium mapping xenibase.test to the host. The first test goes from the setup wizard to a database a pg client reaches over TLS with a certificate issued by Pebble; it saves the session, and the rest reuse it in order (mode: "serial", one worker, no retries). Every screenshot point also runs axe in both themes, and a serious or critical WCAG 2.1 AA violation fails the run (a11y). On failure the job uploads Playwright traces.

    test-docs clones the commit into a scratch directory, extracts the shell blocks that docs/install.md marks with <!-- docs-test -->, runs them as written, checks the installer printed a setup code and wrote .env at mode 600, then runs the first e2e test against what it installed. test-upgrade installs UPGRADE_FROM (default v4.1.0), commits a migration that cannot run and tags it, checks that upgrade.sh exits 2 with the old version, schema and a canary row intact, then upgrades to this commit under an annotated test tag and checks the reported version, the schema, the canary and the kept backup.

    Note

    The rehearsal's comment calls v4.1.0 "the previous Xenibase release", but CHANGELOG.md records four since. The upgrade a real install makes next is a subset of the one rehearsed, so the migrations are covered, by a longer path.

    Lint and the race detector#

    .golangci.yml is golangci-lint v2: the standard set (errcheck, govet, ineffassign, staticcheck, unused) plus bodyclose, errorlint, gocritic, misspell, revive and unconvert, and the gofmt and goimports formatters with the module as the local import group. Generated files are excluded strictly, as are the comments and std-error-handling presets. There are 27 //nolint directives, each with a reason. Lint covers the main module only: sdk/go gets go vet in test-sdk, and test/acmedns gets nothing. The UI has no ESLint; tsc -b is its only static check.

    The package tests, the integration and isolation suites and the Go SDK run under -race. test-acme, test-acmedns, the load test and the full move do not.

    Generated code#

    GeneratorFromToVersion pinned by
    oapi-codegen (server)api/openapi.yamlinternal/api/genThe tool directive in go.mod
    oapi-codegen (client, used by the CLI and tests)api/openapi.yamlinternal/api/clientThe same
    sqlcinternal/store/queries, the migrationsinternal/storego run …/sqlc@v1.30.0
    openapi-typescriptapi/openapi.yamlweb/src/api/schema.d.tsweb/package-lock.json

    Generated files are committed. CI regenerates them and fails on any difference in those paths:

    git diff sees only tracked files, so a newly generated file that was never committed would not show. The build catches that case whenever anything uses the new code, which leaves only unused output unchecked. The SDKs are written by hand; the row types an app uses with them come from the user's own schema through xenibase gen types (internal/typegen), not from this repository.

    Versions and the release#

    Every binary carries its version, commit and build date in internal/version, set at link time by LDFLAGS. The Makefile takes the version from git describe --tags --always --dirty and the commit from git rev-parse --short HEAD; the release workflow passes the tag as VERSION. The Dockerfile takes VERSION and COMMIT as build arguments, which install.sh fills from the checkout, so a bundle install reports its tag too (the upgrade rehearsal checks it).

    A tag starts release.yml. It runs make release: the UI, then xenibase-server, -agent and -status for linux amd64 and arm64, the CLI for linux, darwin and windows on both architectures, a source tarball from git archive HEAD, and SHA256SUMS. It checks that the amd64 server embeds the real UI and that the server and CLI report the tag, extracts the tag's section from CHANGELOG.md (failing if it is empty), and publishes with gh release create --verify-tag. xenibase-edge is not among the binaries: the edge and every other image are built from source on the host by install.sh and enable-services.sh, and no image is pushed to a registry.

    Risk

    A release is published whether or not CI passed on its commit. release.yml and ci.yml both start on the same tag push and do not wait for each other; the release job runs no tests, only -require-ui and two version checks. A tag on a commit whose ci, e2e or upgrade job then fails still produces a public GitHub release with binaries and checksums, typically before those jobs finish. deploy.yml refuses such a tag for Xenibase's own server, but anyone installing from the release page, and every CLI user, gets the untested build. The binaries are built from the tagged commit (the checkout is the tag, --verify-tag holds), so the gap is untested code, not foreign code. Fix: run the release as a job in ci.yml with needs: [ci, e2e, docs-install, audit, upgrade] and if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v'), or publish as a draft and promote it after the check-run test deploy.yml already uses.

    The documentation site#

    docsite.Build renders every Markdown file under docs/ (including this atlas's README) with goldmark and GitHub-flavoured Markdown, wraps each in one template with the navigation from docs/site.json, and writes a search.json index (title, section, headings to level 3, and the first 4,000 characters of text). fixLink rewrites links: .md becomes .html, a directory becomes its README page, and anything that leaves docs/, or is a file under it that is not a page, becomes a link to the repository at blob/main. Every internal link must reach a page and its anchor a heading; cmd/docsite lists every broken one and exits 1, and TestDocs builds the real docs in make test-go as well.

    Search is a small script with no dependencies. It loads search.json on the first keystroke, ranks title over heading over body matches (every word must match), and builds results with textContent, so a title cannot inject markup. The renderer passes raw HTML in Markdown through (html.WithUnsafe()); the input is the repository's own docs, so that is a choice, not an exposure. The site is uploaded as a CI artefact and published nowhere by the workflows.

    What the link check does not see

    Links rewritten to the repository are not checked: a guide that links ../deploy/compose/upgrade.sh keeps building after the file moves. At the verified commit all 75 such links resolve (checked by hand for this page). Links written in raw HTML are not checked either.

    The SDKs#

    Three SDKs in sdk/ share one shape (decision V4-M36 #7): a client from the project URL and a key, with data, auth, storage and realtime; a refresh a minute before expiry, one at a time; reads by URL when the URL form can express them and by the JSON query form otherwise; live() queries that refetch on changes, on resync and after a reconnect; and realtime over the Phoenix protocol the edge serves.

    SDKPackage and versionDependenciesUnit tests (make test-sdk)
    JavaScript@xenibase/client 0.1.1, ESM and CommonJS from one sourceNone at run time; TypeScript and Vitest pinned exactlynpm ci, tsc --noEmit, 12 Vitest cases
    Gogithub.com/israel-duff/xenibase/sdk/go, Version = "0.1.0", its own modulecoder/websocketgo vet, go test -race
    Dartxenibase 0.1.0http, web_socket_channel, crypto; no lockfile committed (usual for a Dart library)dart analyze, test/unit_test.dart. Skipped with a message when dart is not on the path; CI installs it.

    The live tests need a project. TestSDKs enables backend services on one, starts an edge behind a proxy that supplies the project's host name, and runs all three (sign-in and refresh, reads and writes under row-level security, a realtime change, files, errors, sign-out). Each skips, or exits 0, without XENIBASE_SDK_URL, which is how make test-sdk runs them harmlessly.

    A secret key (xb_sec_…) makes the JS client sessionless: no storage, no refresh, no reading of the URL (XenibaseClient). The SDK does not stop a secret key being used in a browser; the edge does, refusing a secret key on any request with an Origin header unless the project allows it (secret_key_in_browser). By then the key has been shipped in the app, so the guides tell developers to use the publishable key in apps.

    Versions are set by hand in each package. A JS test keeps VERSION equal to package.json (the test); the Go and Dart constants have no such test. Nothing in CI publishes to npm or pub.dev, and the repository has no sdk/go/v* tags, so go get of the Go SDK resolves to a pseudo-version of the default branch.

    The CLI#

    xenibase is cmd/cli calling cli.App.Run. It has 113 commands that call the API, plus version, as a tree of names (xenibase backup restore, xenibase auth users ban), each over the generated client. Every command takes --json; destructive ones need --confirm <name>; exit codes are 0, 1, 2 for usage, 3 for a failed operation and 4 for 401 or 403. Global flags (--json, --context, --server, --no-wait) are taken from anywhere on the line.

    Login. login runs the device flow (print a code, open the browser, poll at the server's interval), and the user approves in the web app, choosing the organisation and scopes; --token - reads a token from standard input instead. It then stores a context named after the host and the organisation's slug. logout revokes the token on the server unless --keep-token.

    Contexts and the config file. $XENIBASE_CONFIG_DIR, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/xenibase or ~/.config/xenibase holds config.toml (contexts with server, organisation id, token or token_cmd, token id and CA file) and credentials.toml (personal database URLs, cached because the server shows a password once). Both are written at mode 600 in a directory created at 700; saveConfig writes a temporary file and renames it, and a unit test checks the mode. token_cmd runs through sh -c, so a token can live in a password manager. XENIBASE_CA_FILE or --ca-file adds a CA to the system roots for a server with a private certificate.

    Which server and token. resolve starts from --context, XENIBASE_CONTEXT or the current context, then lets the environment and flags override parts of it:

    Risk

    --server or XENIBASE_SERVER sends the current context's token to another host. When a context is selected, resolve takes its server and token, then replaces only the server from XENIBASE_SERVER or --server; the token is replaced only when XENIBASE_TOKEN is set. So xenibase whoami --server https://staging.example, or a CI job that sets XENIBASE_SERVER on a machine with a logged-in context, sends Authorization: Bearer with the production token to the other host. Reproduced for this page with a scratch test in internal/cli: a context for https://prod.example and whoami --server <test server> delivered Bearer xb_prod_secret to the test server. A typo or a hostile URL pasted from a guide is enough. Separately, login accepts http:// for any host, so a token from the device flow can travel and be stored for a plain-HTTP server. Fix: when the server is overridden and differs from the context's, drop the context's token (require XENIBASE_TOKEN or a context for that server), and accept http:// only for loopback addresses.

    Integration tests build the real binary and run it against a real control plane: a CI-style job with a project-restricted write token that runs SQL on its project, gets not-found for another organisation's project and exit 4 deleting its own (M10's done-when); a device login approved as the user, whose saved context is then used; and policies lint exiting 1 while a table has no row-level security (cli_test.go). The e2e journey approves a CLI device login in the browser.

    The brand in code#

    internal/brand holds the name, tagline, colours and logo paths for what the server renders itself: email (mail/layout.go) and documents. Email cannot use CSS variables, so the colours are literal #rrggbb strings. The web app's tokens live in web/src/styles.css, and TestThemeMatchesTheEmailPalette fails when --accent, --accent-strong or --accent-text stop matching Teal, TealDeep and TealLight, or when brand/mark.svg stops using Glow. The other four colours (mint, ink, muted, line) are not compared. brand/render.mjs renders the SVGs to the PNGs in web/public with Playwright's Chromium; it is run by hand and the PNGs are committed. The docs site has its own palette in siteCSS and is not checked against the brand.

    Dependencies#

    One Go module for everything except sdk/go and test/acmedns, at Go 1.26.10, with go.sum committed and oapi-codegen pinned as a module tool. Three npm trees have committed lockfiles and are installed with npm ci: web, test/e2e and sdk/js. The audit job runs on every push (decision M7 #14), so a new advisory against any of them fails every branch until it is dealt with, related to the change or not. There is no Renovate or Dependabot configuration: updates are made by hand.

    Risk

    The audit stops at Go modules and npm packages; the software that faces the internet is in images nobody scans. Production runs Caddy from caddy:2 (a floating tag), PgBouncer from edoburu/pgbouncer:v1.25.1-p0, Postgres on the official images, WAL-G built from a pinned commit with its own Go dependencies, and the Debian or Alpine layers under them. None is checked by govulncheck or npm audit, and nothing proposes updates, so a PgBouncer or WAL-G advisory reaches Xenibase only if someone reads it. The floating tags also mean two installs of the same release can run different Caddy and base layers. Fix: add an image scan (for example Trivy) of the images make e2e-images already builds to the weekly run, and a Dependabot or Renovate config for Go, npm, Docker base images and GitHub Actions.

    The atlas job#

    This atlas is checked by the atlas job: every x-ref, x-code, x-stat and x-page on every page must resolve at the pushed commit, and a pull request that changes the atlas's sources must also change site/index.html. How pages are written, checked and marked stale is on How the atlas is maintained.

    What catches what#

    A change that…Is caught byNot caught when
    Breaks a unit or database test, or racesci: make test-go under -race with Postgres 18The test needs a variable CI does not set (XENIBASE_TEST_PG_BIN, XENIBASE_TEST_DOCKER)
    Breaks provisioning, isolation, HA, backups, servicesci: the integration and isolation suitesA host condition makes a test skip (CPUs, a missing tool)
    Breaks the UI or the install as a user meets ite2e, docs-install; axe in both themesThe journey does not visit that screen
    Breaks an upgrade or its rollbackupgrade; test-deploy with a fake Docker on every pushThe branch is not feat/deploy…: the real rehearsal waits for the weekly run or the tag
    Changes the API without regeneratingcheck-generated; TestEveryRouteDeclaresAnAction for a route with no ruleThe new generated file is untracked and unused
    Breaks a docs link or anchordocs-site and TestDocsThe link points outside docs/ or is raw HTML
    Breaks an SDK against the edgeTestSDKs (all three, live)A subtest skips because node or dart is missing, which does not happen in CI
    Pulls in a known-vulnerable dependencyauditIt is in a container image, a Dart package, or rated below high on npm
    Ships a release with failing testsNothing before publishing; deploy.yml before Xenibase's own serverAlways, for anyone installing from the release page

    Where the specs and the code disagree#

    Spec and code differ
    • V1 §13 and §11.5 run the integration suites with testcontainers-go. They run against the dev compose environment (deploy/dev/compose.yaml, --profile test) started by the Makefile, with the variables in deploy/dev/test.env.
    • V1 §11.5 describes a single workflow: lint, tests, "frontend lint", the generated-code check, builds, integration, Playwright on tagged builds, and release artefacts on tags. There are four workflows; the release is a separate one that does not wait for CI; Playwright runs on every push, not only on tags; and the UI has no linter beyond tsc.
    • V1 §11.5's make release "builds the Postgres image, produces the Compose bundle". It builds neither: the bundle is a source tarball, and every image is built on the host at install time.
    • V1 §11.5's layout lists test/fixtures. There is none; the Supabase-shaped fixture is test/e2e/supabase-fixture.sql and the integration sources are containers in the dev environment.
    • V2 §7.1's config stores the organisation's slug as org; the code stores its id.
    • V4 §8.1's Go SDK is a separate xenibase-go repository; it is sdk/go in this one.

    Part Z · About

    How the atlas is maintained

    Where the atlas's pages live, how the build reads the code, how to tell which pages the code has moved under, and how to update and publish it.

    What it is made of#

    The atlas lives in docs/atlas next to the code it describes, so a change to one can come with a change to the other in the same pull request.

    PathWhat it is
    pages/*.htmlOne file per page: a JSON header, then the page's HTML. The file name only sets the reading order on disk. The header's part and order set the order in the atlas.
    partials/*.htmlDiagrams used on more than one page or too long to keep inline. {{uid}} in a partial is replaced each time it is included, so marker ids never clash.
    src/The shell, the stylesheet and the page script that every page shares.
    atlas.jsonThe title, the repository URL that code links point to, the parts, where the packages live ("packages": {"root": "internal"}), and what each x-stat counts.
    atlas.mjsThe build. Node 22 and git, no packages.
    site/index.htmlThe built atlas: one self-contained file. Open it from disk or serve it anywhere. It is committed, so reading it never needs a build.

    A page's header#

    Every page starts with a comment holding JSON:

    • verified is the commit the page was last checked against, line by line. Set it only after reading the code at that commit.
    • sources are the files and directories the page describes. A commit that touches any of them after verified marks the page as moved.
    • status: "planned" with a scope list renders a placeholder that says what the page will cover.

    Elements that read the code#

    The build replaces these elements before writing the page. Anything that names code is resolved against the working tree, and links are pinned to the commit that was built.

    ElementBecomes
    <x-ref path="…" symbol="…">text</x-ref>A link to the first line in the file containing symbol. Without symbol, a link to the file. A path ending in / links to the directory.
    <x-code path="…" start="…" [end="…" | lines="n"] [doc] [max="n"] [caption="…"]/>An excerpt with highlighting and line numbers. It starts at the first line containing start and runs to the line containing end, or for n lines, or by default to the brace that closes the block. doc includes the comment above it.
    <x-packages names="a,b"/>, <x-packages rest/>Package cards with size and doc comment, read from the code. A bare name is looked up under the package root in atlas.json (internal/); a name with a slash is a path. rest lists every package under the root that no other x-packages mentions, and the build reports it.
    <x-stat name="…"/>A number counted from the repository, as atlas.json's stats defines it: go-lines-nontest, packages, migrations, migrations-latest, api-operations and others. Each definition names one of the kinds in statKinds (lines of tracked files, packages, files in a directory, the latest of them, pattern matches in a file, a captured value, the schema left by replaying migrations).
    <x-page id="page[--section]">text</x-page>A link to another page or section, with the page's title when there is no text.
    <x-include name="file.html"/>A partial.

    Attribute values are matched literally. Write &quot; for a quote inside one, as in start="if is(&quot;worker&quot;) {", and &lt;, &gt; and &amp; for <, > and &: a raw > ends the element, and the build reports what it leaves unexpanded.

    The page script also understands a few classes: callout drift for spec and code that disagree, callout risk, callout note, evt for an event name, stepper with stage items whose data-lit lights the diagram groups marked data-stage, and data-go="page" on any diagram group to make it open that page.

    Keeping it current#

    Run these from the repository root:

    CommandWhat it does
    make atlasBuilds docs/atlas/site/index.html and docs/atlas/dist/artifact.html, and prints every reference that no longer resolves.
    make atlas-staleLists each written page and how many commits have touched its sources since it was checked, with the files.
    node docs/atlas/atlas.mjs checkBuilds in memory and fails if any reference is broken. Use it before committing.

    To bring a page up to date: run make atlas-stale, read the diff of the listed files since the page's verified commit, change what the page says, set verified to the commit you checked, then rebuild. Code excerpts and line links update themselves. Prose, tables and diagrams are what need a person.

    What the checks cannot see

    An excerpt anchored on a symbol keeps working when the code around it changes. A broken anchor is reported, but a change in meaning is not. And a later migration that changes what an earlier one created is not noticed while the excerpt points at the earlier one. That is why each page also lists its sources and turns amber when they change.

    Publishing#

    site/index.html is the atlas. Commit it with the change that updated a page. dist/artifact.html is the same atlas without the document wrapper, for hosts that add their own, such as a claude.ai artifact. It is not committed. CI's atlas job runs node docs/atlas/atlas.mjs check on every push, and on a pull request fails when pages, partials, the build or atlas.json changed without a rebuilt site/index.html.
